messages.text:
Campaign brief: Wickhold Leashgate general availability
From: Ilse Varga-Holm, VP Marketing
Date: October 20, 2026
Status: Approved to plan. Internal until launch day
Reviewers: Noor Eskelund (audience, goal, voice), Priit Salonen (claims), Dov Achterberg (technical read), Kofi Anselm (developer content, X)
What is happening
Wickhold Leashgate reaches general availability on Tuesday, January 26, 2027. Product and Legal have confirmed the status change, and this brief is Product Marketing's announcement of it for everyone working on the campaign.
Two things follow from that.
The early access label comes off for this campaign. Every asset below publishes on or after January 26, so it says "Wickhold Leashgate" on first mention and "Leashgate" after that, with no early access label. On launch day it is correct to say Wickhold Leashgate is generally available. The label rule in the 2026 release notes, the early access wording in the messaging house and the Leashgate section of the approved claims all stay in force for everything else until January 26. Those documents get updated for launch. Where one of them conflicts with this brief on Leashgate's status alone, this brief wins for these assets. On anything else, they stand.
Nothing external mentions general availability or the date before January 26. No teasers, no "coming soon", no countdown. Early access copy already in market stays as it is until launch day.
General availability changes the status of the product and not its scope. Leashgate at launch is what the product overview and the 2026 release notes describe: agent identity, tool-call policy, and the blast radius report, with a gateway running as a sidecar or as a shared Deployment, for agents that make tool calls over HTTP or MCP. Approvals can be answered from Slack. The tie-in that lets Leashgate ask Wickhold Quenchline for a containment action is optional, off by default, and needs Quenchline on the node.
Goals
The numbers here are internal and do not go in copy.
Customers hear it from us first, on launch day, with enough detail for a platform team to judge whether it applies to them.
60 demo requests by March 31, 2027 from teams with an agent running against real tools, in staging or production.
Get the blast radius report into security reviews. We want platform leads to bring it to their next one, as the answer to "what is the worst this agent could do on a bad day?" Sales will track how often it comes up on calls.
Audience
Primary: platform leads who have been asked to get an agent into production and have a security review standing in their way. They already have the concern, and the budget conversation has started. They read docs first, want the failure behavior early, and trust a config snippet over a paragraph.
Secondary: security leaders and security architects writing internal rules for agent use. They need something more enforceable than a policy document. Lead with the decision they have to make. No humor for this group.
Existing customers get the news first, through the technical customer list. Several asked about agents at Slow Burn Summit, and most were not running any in production yet, so do not write as if they all are.
Keep these audiences apart. Platform and security leadership are separate email lists, and they stay separate here. The landing page is written for platform leads. Security leaders get their own email and the launch post.
Key messages
Treat an agent as a workload with credentials, and give it a boundary. This is pillar 3 of the messaging house and the argument under everything else. Talk about tool calls in a cluster. Leave the future of work to other people.
What it does. Leashgate gives each agent an identity, checks every tool call against a tool-call policy, writes a decision record, and reports the blast radius of an agent, including any route around the gateway.
The outcome statement. Leashgate "limits what a compromised agent can do". Use those words exactly.
For platform leads. defaultAction: deny. Your agent framework stays the same. Leashgate fails closed, so an outage of the gateway stops the agent's tools, and teams need to plan for that. Say so plainly.
For security leaders. Before an agent goes live, know its blast radius. Every decision leaves a record your team can read in a security review.
What it does not do. Leashgate sees tool calls, and it does not read or judge prompts. It runs on Kubernetes only, and frameworks that call tools in-process, with no network hop, are out of scope. Being plain about this is part of the pitch.
Channels and assets
Eleven assets, on owned channels only. This is my starting list, so if the mix is wrong, say so when you bring the plan on November 6. The release note, press and sales enablement run separately and are not part of this brief.

Constraints
Claims. The approved claims and the certification sheet apply as usual. Only the status of Leashgate changes.
Proof. There is no customer proof for Leashgate and there is no lab figure for it. Do not name early access partners, quote them or count them. Do not quote a latency figure, since we have none. The Lowmoor Credit Union and Ostler Grocers results belong to other products and do not go on Leashgate assets as if they were Leashgate results. A thin page beats a borrowed number.
Market framing. Use figures from the Wickhold Containment Report 2026, or a fresh third-party statistic with its source. Web research is welcome where it helps, under the usual rules for third-party figures.
Pricing. Pricing after early access is not settled, and I am handling the pricing page separately before launch. Do not state a price or a tier for Leashgate in any asset. Link to the pricing page where a reader needs it, and send buying questions to sales.
Support terms. Say nothing about SLAs or support levels. Those live in the order form.
Roadmap. Describe what the product does on launch day. No future features, no adapter lists, no dates beyond the launch itself.
Competitors. Leashgate stays out of competitive positioning. No comparisons and no comparison blog in this campaign.
Code in copy. Excerpts of ToolCallPolicy rules are welcome. Leave out the apiVersion line, build numbers and the install command. The early access versions do not carry over, and Kofi adds the final block at the paste test.
Images. Use the library. Design's console screens for launch will not be ready in time, and the Leashgate console screens in the library carry the early access pill, which is not to be cropped off. Keep them off every asset in this campaign. The landing page hero is a working room.
Maren's post. It is a draft for her to rewrite. Do not schedule it, and do not assume a yes.
Questions come to me. Anything that touches the claims goes to Priit first.
Ilse

Customers hear it from us first, on launch day, with enough detail for a platform team to judge whether it applies to them. 60 demo requests by March 31, 2027 from teams with an agent running against real tools, in staging or production. Get the blast radius report into security reviews. We want platform leads to bring it to their next one, as the answer to "what is the worst this agent could do on a bad day?" Sales will track how often it comes up on calls.

topic_details.heading: Audiences
topic_details.content: Primary: platform leads who have been asked to get an agent into production and have a security review standing in their way. They already have the concern, and the budget conversation has started. They read docs first, want the failure behavior early, and trust a config snippet over a paragraph. Secondary: security leaders and security architects writing internal rules for agent use. They need something more enforceable than a policy document. Lead with the decision they have to make. No humor for this group. Existing customers get the news first, through the technical customer list. Several asked about agents at Slow Burn Summit, and most were not running any in production yet, so do not write as if they all are. Keep these audiences apart. Platform and security leadership are separate email lists, and they stay separate here. The landing page is written for platform leads. Security leaders get their own email and the launch post.

topic_details.heading: Messages and required wording
topic_details.content: Treat an agent as a workload with credentials, and give it a boundary. This is pillar 3 of the messaging house and the argument under everything else. Talk about tool calls in a cluster. Leave the future of work to other people. What it does. Leashgate gives each agent an identity, checks every tool call against a tool-call policy, writes a decision record, and reports the blast radius of an agent, including any route around the gateway. The outcome statement. Leashgate "limits what a compromised agent can do". Use those words exactly. For platform leads. defaultAction: deny. Your agent framework stays the same. Leashgate fails closed, so an outage of the gateway stops the agent's tools, and teams need to plan for that. Say so plainly. For security leaders. Before an agent goes live, know its blast radius. Every decision leaves a record your team can read in a security review. What it does not do. Leashgate sees tool calls, and it does not read or judge prompts. It runs on Kubernetes only, and frameworks that call tools in-process, with no network hop, are out of scope. Being plain about this is part of the pitch.

topic_details.heading: Campaign scope and channel context
topic_details.content: Eleven assets, on owned channels only. This is my starting list, so if the mix is wrong, say so when you bring the plan on November 6. The release note, press and sales enablement run separately and are not part of this brief.

topic_details.heading: Landing page requirements
topic_details.content: The landing page is the product page, so it has no end date. Use the existing product layout. Its main action is "Book a demo", with a secondary link to the docs for readers who are not ready for a form. A visitor arrives from one of the emails, a social post or the docs, and needs to see what the product does and how it fails.

topic_details.heading: Timeline and dependencies
topic_details.content: 2026-11-06: Asset plan agreed with me, and Noor's OK on audience and goal. 2026-12-11: Outlines for both blog posts to Kofi. 2027-01-08: All drafts in. 2027-01-15: Claims check back from Priit. Page copy to the web team. Maren's draft to Maren. 2027-01-21: X posts to Kofi for review and scheduling. 2027-01-26: Launch. Release note, landing page, customer email, LinkedIn, X. 2027-01-27: Launch post and prospect emails, one day after customers and after the release note. 2027-01-28: Second company LinkedIn post. 2027-02-02: How-to post and its X post. Kofi moves both to February 3 if a release note lands on the 2nd. 2027-02-09: Two-week check on the landing page form. 2027-03-31: Read the goals.

topic_details.heading: Claims, proof and market framing
topic_details.content: Claims. The approved claims and the certification sheet apply as usual. Only the status of Leashgate changes. Proof. There is no customer proof for Leashgate and there is no lab figure for it. Do not name early access partners, quote them or count them. Do not quote a latency figure, since we have none. The Lowmoor Credit Union and Ostler Grocers results belong to other products and do not go on Leashgate assets as if they were Leashgate results. A thin page beats a borrowed number. Market framing. Use figures from the Wickhold Containment Report 2026, or a fresh third-party statistic with its source. Web research is welcome where it helps, under the usual rules for third-party figures.

topic_details.heading: Pricing, support, roadmap and competitors
topic_details.content: Pricing. Pricing after early access is not settled, and I am handling the pricing page separately before launch. Do not state a price or a tier for Leashgate in any asset. Link to the pricing page where a reader needs it, and send buying questions to sales. Support terms. Say nothing about SLAs or support levels. Those live in the order form. Roadmap. Describe what the product does on launch day. No future features, no adapter lists, no dates beyond the launch itself. Competitors. Leashgate stays out of competitive positioning. No comparisons and no comparison blog in this campaign.

topic_details.heading: Code and image requirements
topic_details.content: Code in copy. Excerpts of ToolCallPolicy rules are welcome. Leave out the apiVersion line, build numbers and the install command. The early access versions do not carry over, and Kofi adds the final block at the paste test. Images. Use the library. Design's console screens for launch will not be ready in time, and the Leashgate console screens in the library carry the early access pill, which is not to be cropped off. Keep them off every asset in this campaign. The landing page hero is a working room.

### Leashgate naming: early access label

Added by the release manager at Product Marketing's request, since release notes get quoted more than anything else we write.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate enters early access
results.content:
---
title: Wickhold Leashgate enters early access
date: 2026-05
author: Wickhold product marketing
tags: [leashgate, ai-agents, product-news]
---

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
results.content:
# Wickhold Leashgate

*Product marketing overview for the May 2026 early access. First draft for field and web teams, May 4, updated September 2026.*

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
results.content:
## The short version

Agents are moving from demos into production clusters, and the tools they call are real: a ticketing API, a database, a deploy pipeline, a shell. An agent that reads a poisoned document or a hostile web page can be talked into calling those tools with the permissions its owner gave it. Leashgate prevents prompt injection from becoming an incident. It sits between the agent and its tools, gives each agent a verifiable identity, and checks every tool call against policy before the call goes through.

Runtime policy for AI agents and their tool calls: that is the whole product. It comes from the same place Wickhold Quenchline did. Assume something will go wrong inside the workload, decide ahead of time how far it can go, and make that limit hold on the platform where the workload runs.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
heading_path: Why this belongs to a Kubernetes security company
results.content:
## Why this belongs to a Kubernetes security company

Most of the agents our design partners run are ordinary Deployments with a service account, a few secrets and network access to internal APIs. Their platform teams already know how to reason about a compromised pod. Tool calls are the part they cannot see. From the network, a hostile tool call and a legitimate one look the same: an authorized POST to an internal service.

Early design partner conversations kept returning to one question: what is the worst this agent could do on a bad day? We call the answer the blast radius of an agent. Leashgate exists to measure that and to make it smaller.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
results.content: ## Core concepts

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
results.content:
### Agent identity

Every agent gets an identity tied to the workload rather than a shared API key. Leashgate takes a projected, audience-bound service account token from the pod and exchanges it for a short-lived agent credential, by default valid for 15 minutes. Policies and logs refer to that identity, so "which agent did this" has a precise answer even when ten agents share a framework and a namespace.

Agents acting for a human user can pass that user's identity along. Policy can then require both, so an agent cannot use a tool its current user could not use directly. This is the case design partners ask about most.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
results.content:
### Tool-call policy

A tool-call policy is a declarative rule set, stored as a Kubernetes custom resource. It says which agent may call which tool, with what arguments, how often, and whether a person must approve first.

```yaml
apiVersion: leashgate.wickhold.example/v1alpha1
kind: ToolCallPolicy
metadata:
  name: support-triage-agent
  namespace: support
spec:
  agentSelector:
    matchLabels:
      agent: support-triage
  defaultAction: deny
  rules:
    - tool: tickets.search
      action: allow
    - tool: tickets.update
      action: allow
      arguments:
        status:
          oneOf: [open, pending, resolved]
      rate: 60/minute
    - tool: crm.export
      action: requireApproval
      approvers: [group:support-leads]
      timeout: 10m
    - tool: shell.*
      action: deny
```

`defaultAction: deny` is the default and we recommend leaving it there. Note the `v1alpha1` in the API version: field names may change during early access, and design partners should expect at least one schema migration.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
results.content:
### With Quenchline

Leashgate can ask Quenchline to act. If a policy marks a repeated-denial pattern as suspicious, it can request a containment action, normally isolating the agent pod's network, through the same pipeline Quenchline uses for its own detections. This requires Quenchline on the node. The feature is off by default.

Every decision record goes to the same export path as Quenchline's, so a SIEM rule can correlate a denied tool call with the runtime events around it.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
results.content:
## Walkthrough: the support agent

This is the demo story, and it is the one we use with design partners.

A support triage agent reads incoming tickets and updates them. A customer email contains hidden text telling the agent to export the customer list to an outside address. The agent, doing what agents do, tries it.

1. The agent calls `crm.export` through the gateway. The policy says `requireApproval`, so the call waits.
2. A support lead sees the request in Slack, with the agent identity, the arguments and the ticket that triggered it. They decline.
3. The agent tries `shell.exec` to get at the data another way. Policy denies it, and the gateway returns a structured refusal.
4. After a third denial in a minute, a rule marks the pattern as suspicious. Leashgate requests network isolation from Quenchline, and the pod is contained.
5. The on-call engineer gets a timeline with four decision records and the ticket ID.

The agent was fooled, and the demo does not pretend otherwise. What matters is how little it managed to do afterward.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
results.content:
## What it does not do

- It does not read or judge the model's prompts, reasoning or output. It sees tool calls and their arguments.
- It does not decide whether an allowed call was wise. A policy that allows `tickets.update` allows a bad ticket update.
- It does not cover agents running outside Kubernetes during early access.
- It does not secure the tools themselves. A vulnerable internal API is still vulnerable to any caller.
- It has no published latency figures yet. We are measuring with design partners. Do not quote a number.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
results.content:
## Early access: what partners get

- Named engineering contact and a shared Slack channel
- Monthly policy review with the product team
- Roadmap input on tool adapters and approval workflows
- Support during business hours, Denver time. There is no SLA during early access
- Limit of a small number of clusters per customer, agreed in the addendum

What we ask in return: a named platform owner, a real agent in at least a staging environment, and permission to learn from anonymized policy patterns.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
results.content:
## Open items

- Pricing for Leashgate after early access is undecided. Say it is included with the Enterprise tier for the early access period and leave it there.
- Adapter list for approval workflows is still moving. Slack is working, others are planned.
- Screenshot set for the web page is due from design. The console view is not final, so use diagrams until then.

Questions go to Product Marketing. Noor Eskelund is reviewing naming, and Dov Achterberg is the technical reviewer.

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
# Release notes 2026

Newest first. Maintained by the release manager on the Wickhold product team. Product names follow the name in use on the date of the entry, so anything before March 2 says Tallowatch.

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## Supported versions, as of October 2026

| Product | Supported | Requirements |
|---|---|---|
| Wickhold Quenchline | 5.3, 5.4 | Linux 5.8 or later with BTF, cgroup v2 |
| Wickhold Evenburn cluster collector | 3.8, 3.9 | Kubernetes API access. The cloud collector is hosted |
| Wickhold Leashgate, in early access | Latest build only | Enterprise tier, signed addendum |

Support covers the two most recent minor versions. Upgrades to any version need `helm upgrade` with your existing values unless the entry says otherwise.

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## Deprecations in progress

| Item | Replacement | Ends |
|---|---|---|
| `/v1/tallowatch/` API paths | `/v1/evenburn/` | March 2, 2027 |
| `v1beta2` containment policy API | `v1` | Quenchline 6.0, date not set |
| Syslog over UDP for event export | Syslog over TLS or OTLP | Quenchline 6.0, date not set |

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## October 13, 2026: Wickhold Quenchline 5.4

Quenchline 5.4 adds a per-policy dry run. `kubectl annotate containmentpolicy ledger-api quenchline.wickhold.example/dry-run=24h` runs a contain-mode policy in observe mode for the stated window, then returns it to contain mode. The change is recorded in the policy status so reviewers can see why no containment fired.

- Support for Kubernetes 1.37
- Reduced ring buffer drops on nodes running many short-lived CI jobs
- Fixed: `holdProbes` window ignored when a container had a gRPC liveness probe

Upgrade note: the chart now sets `priorityClassName: system-node-critical` by default. Customers with a resource quota in `wickhold-system` that restricts that class must update it before upgrading, or the DaemonSet rollout will stall.

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## October 6, 2026: Quenchline 5.3.2

Patch release. Fixes a policy sync loop that raised control plane traffic on clusters with several thousand ContainmentPolicy objects. No customer-visible change in behavior apart from lower API load. Customers on 5.3 can skip this and take 5.4.

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## September 30, 2026: final `wickhold/tallowatch` chart

The old chart stopped receiving releases today, as announced on March 2. Existing installs keep working but will fall out of support with the next Evenburn minor release. Metrics with the `tallowatch_` prefix are no longer emitted from Evenburn 3.9.1 on. Update any remaining dashboards and alert rules.

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## September 29, 2026: Wickhold Evenburn 3.9

Evenburn 3.9 improves how exposure paths handle service meshes. Paths now account for mesh authorization policies, so a route the mesh denies no longer appears as open.

- Fix order can now be grouped by owning team, using a label the customer chooses
- New CIS Benchmarks profile for Kubernetes 1.36
- Fixed: drift false positive on fields defaulted by the API server after a version upgrade

Known limit: mesh awareness covers sidecar-based meshes in this release. Ambient-style meshes appear as if no mesh policy exists, so paths may be over-reported.

Upgrade note: the collector needs `get` on mesh authorization resources for this feature. The chart adds them to the ClusterRole, so customers who manage RBAC separately must add them by hand. Without that permission, paths are calculated as before and a console notice explains why.

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## September 15, 2026: Slow Burn Summit release

Shipped during the summit in Denver, September 15–16.

- Quenchline: decision records now link to a replay of the process tree in the console
- Evenburn: new evidence report layout, with one PDF per control family
- Wickhold Leashgate, in early access: blast radius report now flags bypass routes through cluster DNS names, and approvals can be answered from Slack

Replay is the piece people asked about most at the summit. It shows the parent chain, the arguments as redacted by policy, and the containment action on one timeline, and it reads from the same retained events as the rest of the console.

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## August 25, 2026: Leashgate early access build 0.6

Second schema migration of the early access. `spec.tools` is renamed `spec.rules`, with a conversion webhook that handles existing objects. The `v1alpha1` API version stays. Partners running the sidecar mode must restart agent pods so that the injected gateway matches the controller.

- Gateway decision records now include the argument names that failed validation, never the values
- Fixed: requireApproval timeouts returned a 500 in place of a structured refusal

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## August 11, 2026: Quenchline 5.3

- Support for Kubernetes 1.36 on arm64 nodes with 64K pages
- New detection: unexpected `memfd_create` execution
- OTLP export now batches, with `export.otlp.batchSize` to tune it
- Fixed: agent reported `Ready` before LSM hooks were attached

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## August 4, 2026: Leashgate early access build 0.5

- Blast radius report now reads Secret mounts as well as RBAC
- Shared gateway mode, as a Deployment in the namespace, joins sidecar mode
- Known issue: the shared gateway does not yet pass through human-user identity. Partners who rely on that should stay in sidecar mode

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## July 21, 2026: Evenburn 3.8

- Exposure paths now include workload identity bindings across namespaces
- Ignore rules can carry an expiry date
- Cloud collector templates updated. Customers using customized read-only roles should compare theirs against the new template, since three read permissions were added

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## July 7, 2026: Quenchline 5.2.1

Patch release. Fixes `keepDNS` on clusters where the DNS service uses a non-default ClusterIP range, and improves the error message when a pod's cgroup cannot be found during isolation.

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## June 23, 2026: Leashgate early access build 0.4

First schema migration. Argument constraints moved under `rules[].arguments`. Policies need rewriting by hand in this one case, and partners have a migration note from their engineering contact.

- MCP proxy mode now supports multiple upstream servers per gateway
- Human-user identity can be passed through to policy evaluation
- Agent credential lifetime is configurable, default 15 minutes

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## June 9, 2026: Quenchline 5.2

- Isolation refusals for `hostNetwork` pods now raise a console warning when the policy is created, in addition to the record at runtime
- `kubectl get containmentpolicies -o wide` shows mode and last action
- Fixed: event buffer could exceed its 1 GiB limit by one segment

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## May 26, 2026: Evenburn 3.7

- Drift records now show the audit log actor when audit streaming is connected
- Custom checks can match on CRD fields
- Fixed: fix order patches generated the wrong JSON path for RoleBindings with a single subject

results.title: Release notes 2026
results.content:
## May 2026: Leashgate early access build 0.3

Fix release for the first partners. Corrects sidecar injection on namespaces with restrictive pod security settings and adds a readiness gate so an agent pod does not start before its gateway.

results.title: Release notes 2026

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate enters early access
results.content:
# Wickhold Leashgate enters early access

The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report], and that figure comes from incidents involving ordinary workloads with ordinary service accounts. AI agents with tool access are now arriving in the same clusters, and they move faster than the humans on call.

Wickhold Leashgate, our runtime policy product for AI agents and their tool calls, is now in early access. This post explains what early access includes, how the product works, and what it does not do.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate enters early access
heading_path: The problem with agents in production
results.content:
## The problem with agents in production

An agent in a production cluster is a workload that makes its own decisions about what to call next. Platform teams are being asked to run these agents, often with credentials that were copied from a developer's laptop during a pilot. The agent can reach a database, a ticketing system and a deployment pipeline, because during the pilot that was convenient.

Most of the time this works fine. When it does not, the failure is hard to reason about. A model may be manipulated by content it read, or it may simply make a poor decision. Either way, the question for the on-call engineer is the same as for any other incident: how far can this get?

The term we use for that is the blast radius of an agent. It is set by what the agent is allowed to do at runtime, and that is what Leashgate controls.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate enters early access
results.content:
## What Leashgate does

Leashgate sits between an agent and the tools it calls. It works with three concepts.

**Agent identity.** Each agent gets its own identity, separate from the human who launched it and from the service account of the pod it runs in. Logs and policies refer to that identity, so "which agent did this" has an answer.

**Tool-call policy.** A team writes down which tools an agent may call, with which arguments, on which targets. A support agent may read a customer record but may not export a table. A deployment agent may restart a service in staging but may not touch production. Calls outside the policy are blocked and logged.

**Containment.** A call that breaks policy can trigger the same kind of response platform teams already use with Quenchline. If an agent starts behaving badly, it can be cut off from its tools while a human takes a look, and the rest of the application keeps running.

Put simply, Leashgate limits what a compromised agent can do.

A short example of a tool-call policy, in the shape early access customers are using:

```yaml
agent: support-triage
tools:
  - name: crm.read_record
    allow: true
  - name: crm.export
    allow: false
  - name: tickets.update
    allow: true
    when:
      field: status
on_violation: suspend_agent
```

The format may change during early access. We will tell participants before it does.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate enters early access
heading_path: How it relates to what teams already run
results.content:
## How it relates to what teams already run

Leashgate does not replace network policy, RBAC or Wickhold Quenchline, and it should be added to them. Network policy decides which hosts a pod can reach. RBAC decides what a service account can do in the cluster. Quenchline watches processes and connections on the node. None of them can tell that a permitted HTTPS call to the ticketing system was an agent closing every open ticket. That is the layer Leashgate works at: the named tool, its arguments and the identity making the call.

Because the agent's tool calls pass through Leashgate, every call is also logged with the agent identity attached. Several teams in our design conversations cared more about this record than about blocking. When a security reviewer asks what an agent did last Thursday, the team can answer without searching application logs.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate enters early access
results.content:
## What early access includes

Wickhold Leashgate (early access) is available to customers on the Enterprise tier. Participants work directly with our engineering team and get:

- Support for deploying Leashgate alongside an existing Quenchline installation
- Help writing first tool-call policies for one or two agents
- A direct channel to the engineers building the product
- Input on the policy format before it settles

Early access means what it says. Features will change, there will be rough edges, and it should not be the only control around an agent that can reach something critical. We would rather have a small number of teams using it on real agents than a large number of teams trying it in a sandbox.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate enters early access
results.content:
## Who should apply

Early access suits platform and security teams that already have at least one agent in production, or are about to, and have someone who can own policy. Teams still deciding whether to run agents at all should wait. There will be plenty to read as we learn more.

Your account team can tell you more, or you can apply directly.

[Request early access](https://wickhold.example/leashgate)

*Wickhold is the runtime security company for teams that run Kubernetes. Its products contain failures early, so small fires stay small. Founded in 2019 and based in Denver, Wickhold serves more than 140 customers.*

query.query: Leashgate product overview agent identity tool-call policy blast radius report HTTP MCP gateway
query.reason: Verify launch-day product scope, behavior, deployment modes, integrations, and exclusions against product documentation.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
results.content:
### Blast radius of an agent

Leashgate reads an agent's policy, its service account's RBAC and its Secret mounts, then reports what the agent could reach: every tool it may call, each resource those tools touch, and any route around the gateway, such as a direct network path to a database the agent should only reach through a tool. The report is meant to be read in a security review.

```text
AGENT  support/support-triage      identity: spiffe://wickhold.example/ns/support/sa/triage
  tools allowed            2
  tools requiring approval 1
  tools denied             14
  bypass routes            1
    pod can reach postgres.support.svc:5432 directly (no NetworkPolicy)
```

Bypass routes matter more than anything else in that output. A gateway that an agent can walk around enforces nothing.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
results.content:
## How it works

Leashgate has two parts, the gateway and the policy controller.

**The gateway** runs as a sidecar next to the agent or as a shared Deployment in the namespace. Agents point their tool endpoints at the gateway, either over HTTP or as an MCP server that proxies upstream MCP servers. For each call, the gateway verifies agent identity, evaluates the tool-call policy, writes a decision record and forwards or refuses the call. A refused call returns a structured error the agent can read, so a well-built agent can recover or ask for help rather than retry in a loop.

**The policy controller** watches `ToolCallPolicy` objects, validates them and distributes them to gateways. Gateways cache the last valid policy. If the gateway cannot evaluate a call for any reason, it refuses it. Leashgate fails closed, which means an outage of the gateway stops the agent's tools. That is the right behavior for a security control, and teams need to plan for it.

Install is one Helm chart, early access users only:

```bash
helm install leashgate wickhold/leashgate \
  --namespace wickhold-system \
  --set earlyAccess.token="$EA_TOKEN" \
  --set gateway.mode=sidecar
kubectl label namespace support leashgate.wickhold.example/inject=enabled
```

Requirements during early access: Kubernetes, any recent release, containerd, and agents that make tool calls over HTTP or MCP. Frameworks that call tools in-process, as plain function calls inside the agent's own memory, are out of scope unless the tool itself is reached over the network.

results.title: Release notes 2026

## May 2026: Leashgate early access opens

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
results.content:
## Messaging draft

Headline options for the early access page:

- Runtime policy for AI agents
- Know what your agents can reach
- Every tool call, checked against policy

Subhead:

> Wickhold Leashgate, in early access, gives each agent an identity and puts a policy in front of every tool call, so a bad day for one agent stays small.

Platform engineer version:

> One sidecar. `defaultAction: deny`. Tool calls go through a gateway that checks agent identity and arguments, writes a decision record, and refuses anything your `ToolCallPolicy` does not allow. Your agent framework stays the same.

Security leader version:

> Before an agent goes live, you need to know its blast radius. Wickhold Leashgate, in early access, reports what each agent could reach and enforces the limit, with a record of every decision for your auditors.

Bad example, from an early brainstorm:

> AI agents are the next attack surface and the clock is ticking. Is your organization ready?

That is fear with a question on the front of it, and it tells a platform lead nothing. The same goes for anything calling agents "rogue".

results.title: Approved claims, 2026
results.content:
### Wickhold Leashgate (early access)

Leashgate is in early access. Claims describe what the early access product does today. They do not describe a roadmap, and they do not give a date.

Permitted vocabulary is tool-call policy, agent identity, and the blast radius of an agent. The approved outcome statement is "limits what a compromised agent can do".

results.title: Approved claims, 2026
results.content:
## 3. Banned claims

| Do not say | Say instead, or do this | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| "prevents prompt injection" | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Leashgate acts on tool calls. It does not read intent and it cannot promise that an agent will not be manipulated. The claim is false as a matter of product design |
| "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified" | See section 4 | Neither is true |
| "GDPR compliant" | Use the regional rules | Regional wording sits there, and the ban is not limited to that region |
| "breach-proof", "unhackable", "impossible to escape" | Describe the containment action | No security product can support an absolute |
| "zero false positives", "100% detection", "catches everything" | Give a sourced figure or say nothing | We hold no such evidence |
| "guarantee", "guaranteed", "warranty" outside a contract | Remove | These words have legal effect. Service credits live in the order form |
| "the leading", "the fastest", "No. 1", "the only" | Remove, or bring me the comparison data | Superlatives need current comparative substantiation, and we do not hold any |
| "certified by", "endorsed by", "partner of" for any standards body or open-source project | Remove | Using eBPF or Helm is not an endorsement from anyone |
| "saves $X", any return-on-investment figure | Remove | We have no approved financial outcome for any customer |

Two refinements, because they keep coming back:

"Helps prevent" is a banned claim dressed up. A qualifier in front of a promise does not make it a limited promise.

"Compliance-ready" and "audit-ready" were requested in June for a trust page and refused. Wickhold can describe what the product records. Whether a customer passes an audit depends on the customer and the auditor.

results.title: Approved claims, 2026
results.content:
# Approved claims, 2026

Owner: Priit Salonen, General Counsel
Revision 7, 28 September 2026. Replaces revision 6.

This document lists what Wickhold may say about itself, what it may say only with a qualifier, and what it may not say. It governs marketing, sales, developer relations, press and customer success. Founder posts are included. A signature does not change the facts.

If a claim is not listed, it is not approved. That does not mean it is refused. It means nobody has checked it. Send the sentence, the proposed channel and the evidence to priit@wickhold.example. Copy under 500 words comes back within two working days. Reports, press releases and anything with a customer name take five. "Legal said it was fine on a call" is not a record, and I will not recognize it later.

Wording in quotation marks is exact. Do not improve it.

results.title: Approved claims, 2026
results.content:
## 1. Claims approved as written

| Topic | Approved wording | Evidence held by |
|---|---|---|
| Customer count | "more than 140 customers" | Finance, reconciled quarterly |
| Market, time to contain | "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident" | Wickhold Containment Report 2026 |
| Market, median | "the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours" | Wickhold Containment Report 2026 |
| Lowmoor Credit Union | Time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes, 220 nodes | Signed customer approval |
| Ostler Grocers | 63% fewer open critical misconfigurations in 90 days, 1,900 nodes | Signed customer approval |
| SOC 2 | Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026 | Legal |
| Agent policy | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Legal and product |
| Company | Founded in March 2019 in Denver, Colorado | Legal |
| Funding | Series B of $46M in June 2024, led by Marlbank Partners | Legal |

The Containment Report was published on April 14, 2026, and surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. Give the survey size when the copy has room for it. The legal entity is Wickhold, Inc. Contracts, order forms, privacy notices and page footers use that form. Marketing copy uses Wickhold.

results.title: Approved claims, 2026
results.content:
### Customer count

The only approved claim is "more than 140 customers". The following are not approved: "140+ customers", "nearly 150 customers", "hundreds of customers", "thousands of engineers", or any count of nodes, clusters or workloads summed across the customer base. Finance reconciles the number each quarter against active contracts. Pilots, lapsed accounts, open-source users, and companies that attended Slow Burn Summit are not customers for this purpose.

When the reconciled number supports a higher claim, this document will change. Until it does, the number in a sales deck, a conference bio or a partner page is the number here. If you have seen a larger figure in circulation, it is wrong, and I would like to know where you saw it.

results.title: Approved claims, 2026
results.content: ## 2. Claims that need a qualifier

results.title: Approved claims, 2026
results.content:
### Lab figures

Two product figures come from Wickhold's own lab. Both must carry the phrase "in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026", in the same sentence as the figure.

| Figure | Required form |
|---|---|
| CPU overhead | "under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026" |
| Containment speed | "contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026" |

A footnote does not meet this requirement. An asterisk does not meet it. A qualifier on the slide before does not meet it. In a chart, the phrase goes in the chart title or directly under it. In a talk, the speaker says it aloud.

The figures describe a lab, so they may not be presented as field results or customer averages. "Known-bad process" is part of the claim: it does not extend to unknown processes, novel techniques, or "threats" in general. Reports may repeat the figures only if the benchmark year stays attached. When the 2027 benchmarks run, the year changes and this table is reissued. Nobody edits the year by hand.

Approved:

> Wickhold Quenchline adds under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

Not approved:

> Quenchline contains attacks in 38 seconds.

> Under 2% overhead. Guaranteed.

results.title: Approved claims, 2026
results.content:
### Market statistics

Name the source and the year each time. A market statistic in a headline needs its source on the same screen or page section. See section 5 for how long a statistic stays usable.

results.title: Approved claims, 2026
results.content:
### Customer results

Keep the node count with the result. The Lowmoor outcome belongs to a 220-node estate and the Ostler outcome to a 1,900-node estate, and neither may be stated as what a new customer should expect. Do not convert the Lowmoor result into a percentage or a multiple. Nobody approved that arithmetic. Do not combine the two results in one sentence, because that reads as a single program with both outcomes. Which customers may be cited, and how, is covered by the logo and quote policy.

results.title: Approved claims, 2026
results.content:
### Product behavior

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode it records what it would have done. Copy describing automatic containment must therefore be true of contain mode and should say so where a reader could assume otherwise. Containment actions are isolating a pod's network, freezing a process and draining a node. Do not add to the list without product confirmation.

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths and a fix order. It does not change a customer's environment by itself, and copy should not imply that it does.

results.title: Approved claims, 2026
results.content:
## 5. Statistics: 12-month age limit

A market statistic may not be older than 12 months at publication. This is the limit on how old a statistic can be, and it is measured on the day the piece goes out, not the day it was drafted. A post queued in March for release in May is checked against May.

The limit applies to market and survey statistics only. It covers any figure that describes the industry, the market, or a population of teams. It does not apply to customer results such as the Lowmoor and Ostler outcomes, or to product metrics such as the lab figures, which have their own qualifier.

The age of a statistic runs from the publication date of its source. Fieldwork dates do not matter. A report re-quoted in a newer article keeps its original date, so a 2026 article quoting a 2024 survey is a 2024 statistic.

Applied to our own reports:

| Source | Published | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | April 14, 2026 | Usable for publication through April 14, 2027 |
| Wickhold Field Report 2024 | 2024 | Past the 12 months limit |
| Wickhold Field Report 2023 | 2023 | Past the 12 months limit |

The two Containment Report statistics in section 1 are the only market statistics of ours inside the limit today. The Field Report figures still appear in old decks and old posts. That is an archive problem and not a permission. Do not reuse them. Do not reword them to make them feel new, and do not refer to them as "historically" true.

Fresh third-party statistics are allowed without coming to me first, with the source link and the date of the source in the copy. The source must be a named publisher and the figure must appear on the page you link to. A figure found in a vendor's blog, quoting another vendor's blog, gets traced to the original or is dropped. The third party's name still has to clear the competitor rules.

When the 2027 Containment Report is published, section 1 will be updated and the 2026 figures remain usable until they reach the limit. Old assets stay in the archive as they are. They are not re-promoted once a market statistic in them has expired. Paid and email reuse counts as publication.

results.title: Approved claims, 2026
results.content:
## 6. Breach and incident references

This section sets how Wickhold may talk about breaches and other public incidents, in any channel.

1. Never name a victim. That covers company names, product names, and descriptions that identify one ("a large regional retailer in the week it made the news").
2. No humor. Not in the copy, not in the image, not in a speaker's aside.
3. Nothing within 30 days of a public incident. Count from the first public disclosure. For the 30 days, Wickhold does not publish, post, send or sponsor anything that refers to the incident or that is plainly timed to it. An incident is not a marketing hook.

After 30 days, a breach may be discussed in general terms only, as a pattern and without identifying anyone. A technical analysis of a technique is fine if it does not rely on the incident for attention.

The rules cover paid media, social, email, blog posts, sales sequences, talks and replies to journalists. They apply to personal LinkedIn accounts when the post mentions Wickhold or its products. Press inquiries about a live incident go to Ilse Varga-Holm, and nobody comments before she has spoken to me.

If a campaign in market could be read as a reaction to a new public incident, whoever notices it pauses it and tells Ilse. Nobody will be criticized for pausing. Sales may answer a direct customer question about an incident with facts about the customer's own deployment. It may not use the question as an opening.

Incidents at Wickhold customers are never discussed without the customer's written approval, whatever their age. The approved Lowmoor material is the model. It has a figure and no drama.

Not approved:

> After last week's breach at a regional bank, can your team afford another six hours?

Approved, more than 30 days after any related event:

> When a pod misbehaves, Wickhold Quenchline in contain mode can isolate its network while the on-call engineer works out what happened.

results.title: Approved claims, 2026
results.content:
## 7. Rulings from this year

Requests I have already answered. They are listed so that I do not answer them again.

| Request | Ruling |
|---|---|
| "Trusted by more than 140 customers" | Allowed. The count stays exact |
| "Trusted by credit unions" | Refused. One customer is not a plural |
| "Agentless" or "agent-free" for Quenchline | Refused. It uses an eBPF agent. Say so |
| "Lightweight" | Allowed only next to the CPU overhead figure and its qualifier |
| "Real-time" for Quenchline | Allowed for detection. For containment, use the lab figure or leave it out |
| "Stops the attack" | Refused. Name the containment action: isolate a pod's network, freeze a process, drain a node |
| "Automatic remediation" for Evenburn | Refused. Evenburn gives a fix order and people do the fixing |
| "AI-powered" for any product | Refused unless product confirms in writing what the model does. Writing about AI agents does not make the product AI-powered |
| "Secures your AI" or "safe AI" for Leashgate | Refused. Describe tool-call policy and agent identity |
| "SOC 2 certified" | Refused. Say "holds SOC 2 Type II" |
| "Used by your peers" in a sector email | Refused unless a named, approved customer in that sector is shown |
| "Battle-tested" | Refused. It implies a history of incidents at customers that we have not disclosed and may not disclose |

results.title: Approved claims, 2026
results.content:
## 8. Spoken claims, demos and records

Spoken claims count. A webinar is a publication, a sales call can end up quoted in a procurement file, and a recorded conference talk stays available for years. Speakers get the same tables as writers. Questions from the floor that go beyond them are answered with "I will get back to you", and then with an email to me.

Demo environments show synthetic data. A demo may show a containment action in contain mode, and the timing shown on screen is not a claim about customer environments. Presenters should say so if anyone asks. Screenshots from a real customer tenant are not used in any circumstance.

The owner of each asset keeps the published version, or a link to it, and the source for each figure in it for three years. When a claim is withdrawn I will send a list of the assets I know about. I do not know about all of them, so owners should search their own material.

## 9. Review, exceptions, and how this document changes

Every piece of external copy containing a claim from section 1 or 2 is reviewed against this document by its author. Copy containing a new claim, a customer name, or a reference to a security incident also comes to me. Press releases and the annual report come to me regardless.

Exceptions are given in writing, for one asset, and expire with that asset. I have given two this year. Neither should be taken as a precedent.

If this document disagrees with a guideline, a playbook, a deck or a comment from a senior colleague, this document wins. If it disagrees with reality, tell me, and I will change it.

Reviewed each quarter with Ilse Varga-Holm and Noor Eskelund.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate
results.content:
## Who to talk to first

Platform leads who have been asked to get an agent into production and have a security review standing in their way. They already have the concern and the budget conversation under way. The secondary contact is a security architect writing internal rules for agent use, who needs something more enforceable than a policy document.

Avoid leading with AI safety in general. We are selling a control point for tool calls in a cluster. If a conversation moves to model quality or hallucination, say plainly that this is outside what Leashgate looks at.

results.title: Wickhold Leashgate enters early access
results.content:
## What Leashgate does not do

Leashgate does not read prompts and it does not judge whether a model has been manipulated. It has no opinion on the quality of an agent's output, and it will not catch an agent that gives a customer bad advice through a tool it is allowed to use. What it controls is the set of actions available to the agent. A permitted action that happens to be a poor decision will still go through, so policy needs the same care you would give any access review.

results.title: Wickhold opens early access to Wickhold Leashgate, runtime policy for AI agents
heading_path: Wickhold opens early access to Wickhold Leashgate, runtime policy for AI agents
results.content:
# Wickhold opens early access to Wickhold Leashgate, runtime policy for AI agents

DENVER, May 2026 — Wickhold today opened early access to Wickhold Leashgate, a new product that applies runtime policy to AI agents and their tool calls. Early access is included in the Enterprise tier, and teams can apply through their account contact. Wickhold has not set a date for general availability.

Teams that run Kubernetes are starting to give AI agents real work: reading logs, opening pull requests, changing configuration, calling internal services. Those agents act with real credentials, and the tools they call are often the same ones an engineer would use. If an agent is manipulated or simply wrong, the damage depends on what it was allowed to reach.

Leashgate treats an agent as a workload with an identity and a boundary. In early access it provides:

- **Agent identity.** Each agent is identified at runtime, separately from the service or person who launched it.
- **Tool-call policy.** Teams define which tools an agent may call and with what limits. Leashgate applies that policy at the moment of the call and records the decision.
- **Blast radius of an agent.** Teams can see what an agent could reach under its current policy, and narrow it before the agent runs.

Leashgate limits what a compromised agent can do. It does not judge what a prompt says, and it does not make an agent's decisions correct. Those limits are deliberate: the product acts on tool calls, where an agent's actions become real.

"I keep hearing the same thing from platform teams: the agents arrived before the policy did," said Maren Tolliver, CEO and co-founder of Wickhold. "We started this company to keep small failures from becoming big ones. An agent with too many permissions is a small failure waiting for a reason. I'd like teams to have a boundary in place before they need one."

"The design is deliberately plain: deny by default, check every tool call, write down the decision," said Dov Achterberg, CTO and co-founder. "I'd rather give early access teams something narrow that behaves predictably and hear from them about what's missing. There's plenty missing. It runs on Kubernetes only for now, for one thing. That's why it's early access."

results.title: Landing pages
results.content:
## Page skeleton and word budget

| Section | Budget (words) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Hero: headline, one sentence, CTA | 40 | Must make sense with no scrolling |
| Proof strip: customer logos or one number | 25 | One row, no carousel |
| What it does: three blocks at most | 150 | Concrete actions, not themes |
| How it works or how you roll it out | 100 | Steps. Commands if the audience is technical |
| Customer proof: one result, one quote | 70 | A full sentence with the number and the source |
| FAQ: three questions at most | 80 | Real questions from sales calls |
| Closing CTA | 15 | Same action as the hero |
| **Total** | **480** | Leaves 20 words of slack |

CTAs follow the shared CTA format in the email templates. Use one primary CTA per page, repeated at the top and bottom with the same wording. A secondary link is allowed for a technical reader who is not ready for a form, like the docs or the rollout guide.

results.title: Email templates
results.content:
## CTA format for all channels

This lives here because the email team wrote it down first, and it now applies to every channel: email, landing pages, paid, social, the blog, event pages.

A CTA, the call to action on a button or a link, is at most four words, and it starts with a verb. The same CTA wording rules apply wherever the button sits. "Learn more" and "Click here" are banned everywhere, including as link text inside a sentence.

| Fine | Not fine |
|---|---|
| Read the report | Learn more |
| Book a demo | Click here |
| See the rollout guide | Click here to see the rollout guide |
| Request early access | Early access request |
| Save your seat | Your seat is waiting for you |

Say what happens on the other side of the click. "Get started" is allowed but weak, so use something more specific if you can.

results.title: Landing pages
results.content:
## Every page has one job

Before anyone writes copy, the brief answers three things.

- Who lands here, and from where (paid search, a nurture email, a Field Day QR code)
- What they should do next
- What proof they need to do it

A page aimed at both a CISO and a platform engineer ends up serving neither. We build two pages and route by campaign. The rollout guide page for engineers shows commands and flags above the fold. The executive page for the same product leads with what the decision is and what it costs in time.

results.title: Landing pages
results.content:
## Hero copy

The hero says what the product does and who it's for, in that order. Lead with what happens to the reader's workload. Our tagline can sit in the hero of the brand page, but it doesn't describe a product, so product pages shouldn't rely on it.

Good, product page:

> **Contain runtime failures before they spread**
> Wickhold Quenchline detects bad behavior in Kubernetes and isolates a pod, freezes a process or drains a node, under the policy you set.
> [Book a demo]

Good, posture page:

> **Know which misconfiguration to fix first**
> Wickhold Evenburn tracks drift across cloud and cluster, finds each exposure path and gives your team a fix order.
> [See a sample report]

Good, early access page:

> **Set policy for what AI agents can call**
> Wickhold Leashgate, in early access, applies tool-call policy at runtime and limits what a compromised agent can do.
> [Request early access]

Good, report page:

> **The Wickhold Containment Report 2026**
> A survey of 412 platform and security leaders on how long containment takes, and where the hours go.
> [Read the report]

Good, brand page:

> **Small fires stay small.**
> Wickhold is the runtime security company for teams that run Kubernetes.
> [See how it works]

Bad, from a 2025 agency concept:

> **Next-level cloud security for the modern enterprise**
> One powerful platform. Total confidence. Peace of mind at every layer of your stack.

Nothing in that hero says what the software does. It would fit a mattress company if you swapped "stack" for "bed".

results.content:
# Landing pages

**Noor Eskelund and the web team, April 2026.** Written the week the Containment Report page went live, while the mistakes were fresh. Revised May 2026.

This covers campaign pages, product pages, persona pages and report pages on wickhold.example. The docs site and the blog have their own conventions.

results.title: Landing pages
results.content:
## Hard limit

A landing page is 500 words at most. That counts every word a visitor can read on the page: headline, subheads, body, proof, form labels and the FAQ. Navigation and the site footer don't count.

If the page runs over, cut sections. Don't shrink the type or tuck copy into tabs and accordions. It still counts, and the page is still doing too many things. Long-form material belongs in the report, a blog post or the docs, and the page links there.

results.title: Landing pages
results.content:
## Proof

Each number sits with its source in the same block, so nobody has to scroll to a footnote to check it. These are approved as written:

- Lowmoor Credit Union, 220 nodes: time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes.
- Ostler Grocers, 1,900 nodes: 63% fewer open critical misconfigurations in 90 days.
- Under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

Don't round them, combine them or place two customers' numbers in one sentence. One page gets one customer story. Stacking every number we have makes the page feel like a pitch deck, and readers trust a single detailed result more.

results.title: Landing pages
results.content:
## How-it-works blocks

This is where the two audiences differ most. For engineers, show the thing itself. A short command block costs few words and earns more trust than a paragraph:

> **Install in observe mode**
> `helm install quenchline wickhold/quenchline --set agent.mode=observe`
> The agent attaches to each node. Nothing is contained until you change the mode.

For security leaders, give steps in terms of time and ownership:

> **Week one:** Quenchline runs in observe mode on one cluster.
> **Weeks two to four:** Your team reviews what it would have done.
> **After week four:** You decide which namespaces move to contain mode.

Both describe the same rollout. Neither should use a diagram that needs a paragraph to explain it.

results.title: Landing pages
results.content:
## FAQ

Pull questions from sales calls, not from what we wish people asked. Answer in two sentences or fewer. A good FAQ answers the objection that would otherwise stop the form.

> **Will this take down production?**
> In observe mode, Wickhold Quenchline takes no action. You choose when and where contain mode starts.

> **How much overhead does the agent add?**
> Under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

results.title: Landing pages
results.content:
## Matching the ad

Paid pages must repeat the promise of the ad that sent the visitor there, in nearly the same words. If the ad says "fix order for misconfigurations", the headline says it too. Demand gen writes the ad and the hero together, in the same doc, so they don't drift. We clone a page per ad group only when the message differs. One page per keyword produced 60 near-identical pages in 2025, and the web team spent a month consolidating them.

results.title: Landing pages
results.content:
## Forms

- Report pages are ungated as of April 2026. We ran the 2025 report behind a form and sales complained about lead quality for months.
- Demo forms: work email, company, cluster count. Three fields. We tested five, and completions dropped enough that nobody wanted a second test.
- Don't ask for job title. Enrichment handles it.
- The thank-you page tells people exactly what happens next and when. "A solutions engineer will reply within one business day" is what we can actually keep.

results.title: Landing pages
results.content:
## Pricing on pages

Product pages link to the pricing page and don't repeat its contents. Tiers change, and the pages that repeat them never get updated. Paid-search pages for pricing queries can show a short tier summary pulled from the pricing page, reviewed by Priit before launch.

results.title: Landing pages
results.content:
## Build and review

1. Brief, with Noor's OK on audience and goal.
2. Copy in a shared doc with a word count at the top. Over 500 goes back.
3. Claims check by Priit, with sources pasted next to each claim.
4. Design and build. Web team needs five business days for a new layout and two for an existing one.
5. Staging review on a phone first. Most paid traffic arrives there.
6. Launch, then a check at two weeks: is anyone completing the form, and where do they drop off?

Use the existing layouts when you can. We have three (product, campaign and report) and each has been tested for load speed and for the mobile form. A page built from scratch needs a reason, and "it's a special campaign" isn't one.

results.title: Landing pages
results.content:
## Old pages

Any page without traffic for six months gets redirected. Campaign pages get an end date at launch. In the 2026 rebrand cleanup, the web team found pages from 2023 still live and indexed, which is how you end up with a stale claim ranking above the current one. Put the end date in the brief.

results.content:
## The hero

**A landing page hero shows product UI or a working room.** Those two options only.

That excludes illustration from the hero slot, even though we use it heavily elsewhere. Visitors on a landing page are deciding whether Wickhold is real. A screen from the product, or a real room where this work happens, answers that faster than a metaphor.

Use product UI when the page is about a product or a capability. Use a working room when the page speaks to a role or a problem and there is no single screen to show.

| Page | Hero |
|---|---|
| Quenchline product page | Product UI: one containment action |
| Evenburn product page | Product UI: exposure path or fix order |
| Leashgate early access page | Product UI: a tool-call policy, with the early access pill in frame |
| Platform engineering solutions page | Working room, or a terminal-adjacent product view |
| CISO or board-facing page | Working room. No people posing |
| Campaign page for the Containment Report | Working room |
| Event registration | A working session photographed at a past Slow Burn Summit, cleared for this use |

Sections below the hero have more room. Spot illustrations work in feature rows. Check each section's ground, since landing pages usually alternate Tallow and Soot bands, and a `safe_on: light` file dropped in a Soot band disappears. Nav and footer logos need checking band by band as well.

Screenshots in the body can run larger and carry callouts. Keep one image per section at most.

results.content:
## Narrower than the screenshot rules

Product screenshots in general may show a full frame or a crop. In a landing hero:

- **A crop only.** No full-dashboard views. The hero width on a laptop leaves about 700px for the image, and a 1600x1000 frame shrinks to illegible at that size
- **One callout at most.** Up to three are allowed elsewhere
- **A mobile check.** At 390px wide the crop has to show something readable. If it cannot, supply a tighter mobile crop

For working rooms, narrower than photography:

- **No visible screens with content,** so that the eye goes to the headline
- **The photo has to work with the headline beside it.** Type does not sit over the room. The layout is split, or the image sits below

results.title: Landing page imagery
results.content:
## Legal pages carry no people

Terms, privacy, subprocessors, the DPA page, and the like: no people in any image on these pages. That covers portraits, illustrated silhouettes, hands in a shot and a team in the footer strip. The same applies to the legal section of any combined page.

results.title: Landing page imagery
results.content:
## Performance

Hero image under 250 KB on the wire. Serve WebP with sizes set, and do not lazy-load the hero. SVG for logos and icons. Everything below the fold lazy-loads. A slow page is a credibility problem for a company that sells to platform engineers, and they will open dev tools.

results.title: Landing page imagery
results.content:
## Video in a hero

Allowed: a silent loop of a containment action, under ten seconds, with a poster frame that passes the hero rule by itself. Not allowed: a talking-head brand film. We tried one on the old homepage and the bounce numbers were bad enough to end the debate.

results.title: Landing page imagery
results.content:
## Reuse across pages

A/B test variants use the same hero rule. If you test a hero, both arms must pass. An illustration "just for the test" still fails, and test pages have a way of becoming permanent.

Do not use the same working-room photo on two product pages. Visitors move between them, and a repeated picture makes the site look small.

results.title: Landing page imagery
results.content:
## Common hero rejections

| Submitted | Problem |
|---|---|
| Illustration of a wick on the Quenchline page | Good art, wrong slot. Move it to a feature row |
| Full incident page, shrunk | Illegible. Crop to the one action |
| Bright stock-looking meeting room | Fails the working-room test, and it could be any company |
| Product UI floating on a laptop mockup | Adds a second object. Use the crop alone |
| Abstract background with a headline | No product and no room, so it answers nothing |

results.title: Landing page imagery
results.content:
## Open graph and paid variants

Each page needs its own preview image, built from the hero crop. A preview with a product crop needs a larger, simpler view of the same action. Paid campaign pages should reuse the same hero as the ad, so that the click feels continuous.

Region-specific pages use the same imagery unless Legal says otherwise. Do not localize by swapping in a landmark photo.
