**Good source line:** the report name, the year and a link, formatted as the style guide asks.

**Bad source line:** "Source: industry research."

## Review

Data checked by whoever owns the source: product marketing for the Containment Report, Legal for customer results. Brand checks form and color. Do not skip the first of these because the chart "only reuses" a number from an earlier piece.

---
title: Illustration
owner: Brand design
reviewed: 2026-06-18
---

# Illustration

Everything we draw looks like it was cut from paper and laid on a table. That style came out of the rebrand work, and it is deliberately easy to recognize at a small size next to a competitor's glowing network diagram.

## The style

**Flat cut-paper shapes.** Crisp edges with a slight hand-cut irregularity. Layers can overlap. Depth comes from stacking, and the only shadow allowed is a hard offset shape in one flat, darker tone.

**One Ember focal element.** Exactly one thing in the picture is Ember. That is where the eye goes. Everything else is Soot, Tallow, or a small amount of Whetstone or Verdigris.

**On Tallow or Soot.** Those are the only two grounds for finished illustration. An Ember ground removes the focal element, because nothing can stand out from it. Whetstone and Verdigris grounds look muddy.

**No gradients.** None, anywhere: no soft shadows, glows, blurs, mesh fills or textured airbrush. If a shape needs to look lit, cut a second shape. In review, this is the rule most often broken by accident, usually by a shadow effect left on by default in the design tool or by an export that adds banding.

Also out: outlines around shapes, 3D, isometric projection, photographic textures pasted on shapes, and stock vector packs. We tried isometric cluster diagrams in January. They looked like every infrastructure startup's site, and they required a depth that flat paper cannot give.

## What to draw

The brand idea is a wick: the place where a fire is allowed to exist. Use that vocabulary and its everyday relatives.

| Idea | Shapes that work |
|---|---|
| Containment | A ring around a small flame, a tray, a snuffer held above a wick, a firebreak cut through paper grass |
| Isolation of a workload | One tile lifted out of a grid, a pod shape with a paper band around it |
| Posture and drift (Evenburn) | A row of even flames with one leaning, a level, a line of tiles slightly out of true |
| Tool-call policy (Leashgate) | A short tether, a gate latch, a loop of cord around a post |
| On-call | A lamp and a mug, a single lit window in a dark paper building |
| Fix order | Steps cut from paper, three stones across a stream |

Keep the flame small. A small flame contained is the entire idea, and a large one means disaster, so the flame should stay well under a tenth of the frame. If the concept seems to need a wall of fire, the concept is wrong.

Kubernetes has its own visual habit of hexagons and ship wheels. Do not draw the Kubernetes logo, which is someone else's mark. Pods are tiles. Nodes are trays or shelves. Clusters are groups of those on a shared ground.

## People in illustrations

Rarely. When a figure is needed, show a simple paper silhouette with no face, working at something. Do not use characters, mascots or recurring cartoon engineers. We had a proposed mascot in the rebrand round, a little candle with eyes, and we all agreed to pretend it never happened.

## Formats in the library

| Format | Size | `background` | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hero illustration | 1536x1024 | `solid` | Wide placements, full scene with ground included |
| Spot illustration | 1024x1024 | `transparent` | Inline in body copy, feature grids, beside text |
| Abstract background | 1536x1024 | `solid` | Behind type in designed layouts. No focal element |

Hero illustrations already contain their ground. Check whether the file is the Tallow or the Soot version and place it in a section where it does not produce a visible box edge against a slightly different ground. Sample the color: if the layout ground is exactly Tallow or Soot, the edge disappears, which is what you want.

Spot illustrations take on whatever sits behind them, so `safe_on` matters. Many spots use Soot shapes and are `safe_on: light`, and those shapes vanish on a dark layout, leaving a floating Ember fragment. Others are built for dark and carry Tallow shapes. Check the record, look at `variant_of` for a sibling, and preview on the real ground. If an image is `any`, still look for a pale fringe along cut edges on Soot.

Do not put a spot illustration on a photograph. Do not put a spot on an Ember band. Do not put a box behind a spot to make it safe on the wrong ground, because the box will look like a mistake. Use the correct version or ask for one.

Abstract backgrounds exist to carry type. On their own they have no focal point, so they are never published without the layout on top of them.

## Composition

- Hero: focal element off center, with at least a third of the frame quiet. That quiet space is where crops happen.
- Spot: centered, with an even margin. No shape touches the edge of the canvas.
- Scale: one size jump between focal element and supporting shapes. Eleven small shapes around one medium shape reads as confetti.
- Fewer shapes than you think. Most good spots have under eight pieces of paper.

## Color limits

Ember appears once, as a single element. Two separated Ember shapes means two focal points. If the composition needs a second accent, use Verdigris, and keep it small. Whetstone is good for the supporting middle layers on Tallow, although its value is close to Ember's, so it does not provide much separation when placed directly next to the focal element. Leave a Soot or Tallow gap between them.

All colors are exact palette values. Do not use tints of Ember. Tints turn it toward pink and off brand.

## Series

When a piece needs several illustrations, such as a report with chapter openers, vary the object and keep the ground, scale and Ember position consistent. Mixing Tallow and Soot grounds within one piece is fine only if it follows the document's structure, for example one dark chapter opener per part.

## Report covers and chapter openers

Long pieces earn one larger concept. The Containment Report cover uses one cut-paper object at a large scale on Soot, with the title set as live type by a designer. Chapter openers repeat that object in a changed state, for instance the tray filling up or a wick burned further down. This gives a long PDF a thread through it without any extra Ember.

## Concepts that failed in review

| Concept | Why it failed |
|---|---|
| Paper flame in a glass jar | Reads as a candle ad, and the jar needed a highlight, which needs a gradient |
| A fire engine | Cute, and it suggests rescue after the damage is done |
| A forest fire with one saved tree | Too much fire, plus sentimental |
| A dog on a leash for Leashgate | Everyone laughed, then nobody could explain the agent. The tether alone works |
| A map of connected glowing nodes | Off style, and it looks like every other vendor |

## Export checklist

PNG for transparent files, with a real alpha channel. Open the file on Tallow and on Soot, then zoom to 200% on the cut edges. Check that the Ember value samples at `#C2501F`, since color profiles in some export paths move it slightly. Save the editable vector source beside the export and record where it lives.

## Requests and review

Give the designer the idea in one sentence and the placement. Do not sketch the metaphor yourself in the request unless you are sure of it: people usually ask for a shield, and we do not draw those. New illustrations get a review at thumbnail size and at full size on both grounds. Once approved, the file enters the library with a complete record, including `background`, `safe_on` and `variant_of` for any ground-specific sibling.

Good request: "Blog post about draining a node before an upgrade. Calm, procedural."

Bad request: "Something cool and techy with flames and a shield for our big launch!!"

# Photography

Brand team, revised July 2026. The look was set for the rebrand and has not changed. What changed this summer is the section on judging library photos by eye, because we kept seeing the same bad picks in drafts.

## The look

Wickhold photography looks like it was taken by someone who was already in the room.

**Available light.** Windows, overhead tubes, the glow of a laptop, a desk lamp. No strobes, ring lights or colored gels. If a room is too dark for the shot, use a longer exposure or find a better room.

**Warm and slightly underexposed.** Think of the last hour of a working day. Skin tones stay warm and natural. Shadows may go deep, though they should not go black across half the frame. If the image histogram crowds the right side, it is too bright for us.

**Working rooms and real infrastructure.** Equipment rooms, cable trays, network closets, a shared office with coffee rings on the table, a laptop open at a kitchen counter during an on-call shift. Places where the work of running Kubernetes actually happens. The subject of a security company's photo library is the people on call and the things they keep running.

**Honest mess.** Leave the cables. Leave the sticky notes (after reading them). A tidied room reads as staged, and staged reads as an advertisement.

## Subjects we want more of

- Hands on a keyboard, shot from the side, with screens angled away or dark
- Two people talking through a problem at a whiteboard, mid-sentence
- Rack doors, patch panels, labeled cable runs, in warm light
- A notebook with a hand-drawn cluster diagram
- A small team around one laptop late in the day
- The Denver office at the end of the afternoon
- Customer-side infrastructure, once the paperwork is done

heading_path: Stock clichés we do not use
results.content:
## Stock clichés we do not use

These are banned in every Wickhold image, photographs above all:

- Hooded hackers, or any faceless figure at a keyboard in the dark
- Padlocks, physical or floating over a circuit board
- Glowing shields
- Matrix code, or any green-on-black rain of characters
- Blue server-room haze: aisles of racks lit cold blue, usually with fog or lens flare

The reason sits close to the voice. All five say "be afraid" or "we are a generic security vendor", and the brand exists to say neither. An engineer who sees a hooded figure on a Wickhold page will assume the rest of the page is equally lazy.

Close relatives count as the same failure: binary digits projected on a face, a globe wrapped in network lines, a hand reaching toward a holographic lock, a person in a suit pointing at a transparent screen.

## Judging library photos by eye

The library's metadata does not catch everything. Some old or off-brand photos are sitting in the library with an empty `restrictions` field, because nobody ever marked them. Some of them have sensible titles and tags. A clean record tells you nobody objected. You still have to look at the picture.

Open it at full size and ask:

1. **What color are the shadows?** Ours fall warm, toward brown or neutral. If the shadows go blue, it belongs to the 2024 era or to a stock site. The look of that era was bright, cold and very blue, and it clashes hard with Ember on the same page.
2. **Is the light real?** Even, shadowless light across a whole room means a set or a heavy edit.
3. **Is anybody posing?** Direct eye contact with the lens, crossed arms, a group laughing at a laptop: reject.
4. **Could this photo appear on any company's site?** If yes, reject it. We want to see a detail that belongs to this work.

If a photo fails one of these and has no restriction on it, do not use it, and tell Brand so the record can be updated. That second part helps the next person.

Examples from recent draft reviews:

| Draft used | Verdict | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Rack aisle, cold blue light, faint haze, no people | Rejected | Clean metadata, wrong look |
| Woman with headset smiling at the camera in a bright open office | Rejected | Posed and generic |
| Engineer's hands, laptop glow, dim closet behind | Approved | Warm, specific, one focal point |
| Three people at a whiteboard, one mid-gesture, late sun on the wall | Approved | Available light, real moment |

## Photos by setting

**Team and office.** Real desks, real clutter. Aim for moments between people, with one person clearly the focus of the frame. Conference-room shots work when something is happening on the table. The office kitchen works better than the boardroom.

**Infrastructure.** Shoot close. A patch panel with handwritten labels says more than a long aisle. Cables, breakers, fans, a rack door left open. Whatever the room's own lighting does, keep it warm in the edit, and if the room is lit cold and cannot be corrected, get closer to a warm lamp or drop the shot.

**Customer scenes.** The grocery distribution office, the credit union's back room, a store's network closet. These are the most valuable photos we have, since they show Kubernetes and its operators somewhere other than a startup. They also have the most paperwork behind them. A customer scene looks ordinary and that is the point: no hero angles.

**Remote on-call.** Kitchen tables and spare rooms, a laptop at dusk, a phone face-up beside it. On-call happens at home and most stock libraries do not show it. Keep faces turned away unless the person is a signed volunteer.

## Choosing for the audience

The same library serves different readers, so pick with them in mind.

- For platform engineers, prefer detail. A readable (and real) cable label will win more trust than any wide shot. Faces matter less.
- For CISOs, prefer a calm room and a person thinking. The frame should feel like a decision is being made. Skip anything that looks like a crisis in progress, including people crowding a screen.
- For a general or press audience, prefer one clear person doing one clear thing.

heading_path: Comments you will get in review
results.content:
## Comments you will get in review

"Too clean." The room looks unused. Find a frame with evidence of work.

"Whose laptop is that?" A third-party logo or a sticker with a company name is visible. Remove it or pick another frame.

"What's on the whiteboard?" Someone has to read it. Customer names and incident details are the usual finds.

"Cold." The white balance is off. If warming it makes skin go orange, the original light was wrong, so reshoot.

heading_path: What the metadata means for photos
results.content:
## What the metadata means for photos

All photographs carry `background: scene`. A photograph keeps its environment: we do not cut people or objects out of their rooms, and we do not swap the sky through an office window. If you need a subject on a plain ground, you need an illustration.

Most photos are 1536x1024 landscape, with a few 1024x1536 portrait. Check `width` and `height` before you plan a layout around one. Upscaling a photo by more than about 20% shows.

`safe_on` is mostly `any` for photos, since a scene brings its own ground. A photo edge can still fight the layout. A dark, underexposed photo set straight on Soot loses its edges entirely, so give it margin or move it to a Tallow section.

`source` will read `internal-production` for in-house work, and `attribution` is often empty. We do not run photographer credits.

## Cropping

Crops are allowed and usually needed, because different placements want different shapes. Keep the focal point inside the middle two-thirds of the frame, so a further crop by a platform does not cut it off. Do not crop a person at the neck or the wrist. Rotation is limited to straightening a horizon by a degree or two.

## Light editing only

Allowed: exposure, white balance toward warm, gentle contrast, removing a stray sticky note with a password on it, removing a third-party logo from a laptop lid.

Not allowed: adding screens, adding people, removing people from a group shot to work around a restriction, adding atmosphere (smoke, glow, flares), or replacing what is on a monitor with invented UI. If a monitor needs to show the product, use a real capture composited at the correct perspective, reviewed by Brand. We tried fake monitor content in a March shoot and engineers spotted the impossible kubectl output within a day.

Keep the original. Save an edit as a new library record with `variant_of` set to the original, so the restrictions on the source can be traced.

## Shooting new photos

If you are booking a shoot, the brief should cover:

- Named location and who there has agreed to it
- A shot list of six to ten moments, written as things happening rather than as poses
- A warning to everyone to clear whiteboards, sticky notes and screens of customer names, credentials and anything from an active incident
- Who will enter the metadata. Files without a record do not enter the library

Shoot in the afternoon if you have a choice. Morning light in the Denver office is cold, and it takes more work to bring back to our look than it is worth.

Phone photos are welcome if they meet the look. Some of our best library images came from an engineer's phone in a colocation facility. Send the original file, not a screenshot of a chat.

## Things we tried and dropped

**Black-and-white.** Trialed for the founder story in spring. It looked serious and lost the warmth that sets us apart from the rest of the category.

**Ember color wash over photos.** Looked like a concert poster, and it tinted skin badly.

**Close-ups of fire.** One literal candle shot made the rebrand launch. After that the joke was used up, and flames in photographs began to read as disaster. A flame belongs in illustration, where it stays small.

**Drone shots of data centers.** Anonymous, and they could belong to anyone. They also raised a question about which site it was, which we could not answer.

# Product UI screenshots

Product marketing, with design review from Brand. Current as of the September release.

Screenshots are the one kind of image a platform engineer will inspect closely. They will read the pod names and check whether the timestamps make sense. Treat every screenshot as a claim about the product, because that is how it gets read.

## Where screenshots come from

Screens are captured from the product running in the demo environment, or rendered from the demo environment's HTML with Playwright at 1600x1000. Library dashboards are that size and opaque.

Never capture from:

- A customer tenant, even with their permission and even if you blur things
- Our own production tenant, which contains real incidents and real people's names
- A design file. Mockups of features that do not exist are not screenshots. If we need to show something unreleased, it must be labeled as a concept and approved by product marketing and Legal
- A model. Interface images are never generated

Do not paint over or blur a screenshot to hide data. Blurred regions imply the original had something worth hiding. Fix the demo data and take it again.

## Demo data

The demo environment is seeded with fictional clusters, namespaces and workloads. Keep it believable:

- Cluster and namespace names that look like real engineers wrote them: `payments-prod`, `batch-eu`, `ingest`. No `foo`, no `test123`, and nothing funny at a customer's expense
- Container images under `registry.wickhold.example`, so no real image names or registries appear
- People's names, where the screen shows an assignee, from the fictional demo roster. Do not use real staff, because staff leave. No names of customers, approved or otherwise
- Timestamps that agree with each other. An alert cannot be contained before it fired
- CVE IDs only when they are real, public and old. Do not imply a live incident

**Numbers on screen are claims.** A tile that shows a time to contain, a CPU figure or a count of findings fixed will be read as a result. Demo values must not look like a customer result or undercut an approved figure. If a tile reads like a brag, change the seed data, or crop it out. If you want to make a performance point, use an approved claim in the copy and keep it out of the picture.

Pricing and contract screens are never captured. Discount fields, billing pages and node counts tied to a plan stay out of marketing images.

## What to show

Each screenshot shows one action or one finding. That's the focal point, and the crop should make it obvious. Good subjects:

**Quenchline**
- One containment action in progress: isolating a pod's network, freezing a process, or draining a node
- The default containment policy view, with one rule highlighted
- Contain mode and observe mode side by side only if the page is explaining the difference. Otherwise pick one

**Evenburn**
- One piece of drift, showing expected and actual values
- An exposure path from a public entry point to a workload, short enough to read
- A fix order list, top three items

**Leashgate**
- One tool-call policy and the call it blocked or allowed
- An agent identity record
- The early access pill in the product header stays in frame. Do not crop it off

Avoid the whole-dashboard overview shot unless the point is the overview. A full 1600x1000 frame, shrunk to fit a column, is a gray rectangle full of illegible numbers.

## Cropping and framing

- Crop to the region that carries the point. Keep enough surrounding UI so that a reader knows where they are, usually the page title and one neighboring panel
- If UI text is too small to read at the published size, crop tighter or use a different screen
- No fake browser chrome and no device mockups. A floating laptop with a screenshot on it adds a second object and looks like a template
- No perspective tilts or 3D rotation
- Square corners, unless the layout's image style rounds everything equally
- A 1px Whetstone border is allowed when a screen with a light UI sits on Tallow and the edge gets lost

The interface has its own colors and they stay as they are. Do not recolor UI to suit a layout. Do not swap state colors to make something look calmer than it is.

## Annotations

Annotations are added in the design tool, on a separate layer, after the capture. One callout is usually enough, three at the most.

- Callouts use IBM Plex Sans in sentence case
- One Ember ring or arrow marks the focal area. No red boxes, no hand-drawn circles, no numbered badges over the UI
- Describe what happened. "Network isolated in this step" is good. "Instant protection!" is bad
- Commands and flags in callouts use IBM Plex Mono and must be real. Run them first

Example callouts:

| Good | Bad |
|---|---|
| Contain mode freezes the process and keeps its evidence | Stops every attack automatically |
| Drift found on 3 nodes, first in fix order | Full visibility across everything |
| Tool call denied by policy | AI threats eliminated |

## Terminals and CLI output

Engineers often trust a terminal capture over a dashboard. Use a plain terminal at a normal size with IBM Plex Mono, on a Soot background, with the prompt trimmed to `$`. The command has to be real and its output has to be pasted from a real run in the demo environment. Do not edit output to shorten it. Use `...` on its own line if you must cut something, and do so only where the cut changes nothing. Remove usernames, internal hostnames and tokens by fixing the environment and running it again.

## One screen, worked through

The request: show that Quenchline can freeze a process during an incident.

First attempt: the whole incident page at 1600x1000, with the timeline, three tiles, a side panel of pod details and a chat widget from the demo tenant. As a column image it was unreadable, and the one thing that mattered was a small status chip.

Second attempt: a crop to the timeline row showing the containment action and the status chip, with the page title kept above it. One Ember ring on the chip. One callout: "Process frozen, evidence kept". It reads at column width and it says one thing. That is the standard to aim for.

## Keeping screenshots current

Screens age quickly, and old ones do damage in specific ways:

- **Before March 2026, Evenburn screens carry the product's previous name** in the navigation and page titles. Check `added_date` and look at the header. A screen with the old name is unusable, even when the part you want is elsewhere in the frame. Crop-around is not a fix, since the layout and colors are dated too.
- **Before the February 2026 rebrand, the product UI used the old blue theme and the old logo** in the corner. Same answer.
- **Removed features.** Product marketing reviews the library's screenshots against the release notes at each major release, and adds a `restrictions` note to anything that no longer matches.

If a screenshot's record is clean and the picture still looks out of date against the live product, trust your eyes and take a fresh one. The demo environment is reset each Monday, so captures are straightforward. Anything that shows a feature's name, a label or a flow that has changed needs replacing before the next use.

## Metadata for new captures

Every new capture gets a record with `background` set, `source: internal-production`, the product name in `tags`, the release in `description`, and any limits in `restrictions`. If a capture shows a beta feature, say so in `restrictions`, with the date it should be reviewed.

## Video and GIF

Short looping captures follow all of the rules above. Each should show one action from start to finish in under ten seconds. Motion rules sit with the accessibility notes.

## Who signs off

Product marketing checks accuracy. Brand checks the crop and annotations. If a screenshot shows a feature that engineering has not shipped to all customers, the product manager for that area also signs off. Allow two working days.

# Social graphics

For anything designed for a feed: stat cards, quote cards, announcement cards, event cards. A plain photo or a plain chart uploaded to a post is covered by its own category. This page is about designed layouts.

Last touched by the social lead, May 2026. Kofi's team added the engineering post notes.

## Templates first

The library holds a small set of social templates, built in HTML and rendered with Playwright so the type is live and the layout stays exact. Start from one. Copy it, change the content, render it. A file marked as a template is a master and should not be posted unfilled.

Do not rebuild a template in a slide app. That is where off-size margins and the wrong weight of Bricolage Grotesque come from.

If you need a layout the templates do not cover, ask a designer. Do not stretch the stat card to hold a quote.

## Card types

**Stat card.** One number, a short line that says what it measures, and a source. Number in Bricolage Grotesque, very large. Use approved figures only, and keep the wording of an approved stat intact when you shorten it for a card. "7.4 hours" with "median time to contain a runtime incident" beneath it is fine. "Teams are failing at containment" is not what the number says.

**Quote card.** Customer quotes come from approved customers only. Use the quote as approved, without trimming it to sound stronger. Add the name, title and company as they were approved. Portraits are optional, and a portrait has its own consent requirements, separate from approval of the words. Founder quotes follow the same layout.

**Announcement card.** A short headline in sentence case on Tallow or Soot, plus the logo. For a release, name the capability and skip the excitement. "Wickhold Evenburn now shows exposure paths across clusters" is a good model. "Big news coming your way!" is the opposite.

**Event card.** Name, date, city. Slow Burn Summit and Field Day have a shared treatment, set with the events team each year.

## Layout

Each card has one Ember element, and on a card that element is usually a short rule beside the headline or the wick dot. The layout's text is never in Ember. Keep a clear margin all around, because platforms crop and round corners differently.

Logo placement is bottom right on Tallow and Soot cards.

Grounds: Tallow or Soot. Photos may be used in the right-hand half of the split layout, and text never overlaps a busy image. An abstract background from the library is allowed behind type, and it counts as the ground.

Keep the type large. Assume the card is viewed on a phone, in a feed, by someone with a thumb already moving. If you have reduced the font to fit the words, cut words.

## Copy on cards

Cards follow the voice rules with no special allowance for being short. Good:

- Small fires stay small.
- 11 minutes to contain, down from 4 hours.
- Contain mode, explained.

Bad:

- Hackers never sleep. Neither do we.
- The future of cloud security is HERE!
- Is your cluster on fire right now?

The 11-minute line needs Lowmoor named in the post or on the card, so that the number has a source.

A card should not repeat the post word for word. Use the post to expand on the card.

## Engineering posts

For posts aimed at platform engineers, a clean terminal or YAML snippet is often better than a designed card. Set it in IBM Plex Mono on a Soot ground, in a real, tested snippet of no more than twelve lines. Dry humor in a code comment is acceptable. Check the audience first.

```yaml
# drains the node. does not drain your weekend.
spec:
  action: drain-node
  mode: contain
```

Code cards still get checked by someone who can run them. This is a sample of the style, and its field names are not a reference.

## Common rejections

| What came in | What we said |
|---|---|
| Stat with no source anywhere | Add the source in the post or the card, or drop it |
| Ember headline on Tallow | Fails contrast. Use Soot, and keep Ember for the rule |
| Three stats on one card | Pick one. Post the others another day |
| Portrait, quote, logo and a screenshot together | Four focal points. Keep the quote |
| Card reused from before the rebrand | Rebuild it from the current template |
| Customer logo added to a stat card | Needs Legal first. Usually the answer is to name them in the post |

## Timing and thumbnails

Check every card at thumbnail size before you schedule it, and on a dark-theme feed as well as a light one. A Tallow card is a bright rectangle in a dark feed and that works in our favor. A Soot card can melt into the page, so keep its margin clean and its type large. Do not add a border to compensate.

## Series and carousels

We tried multi-slide carousels through Q1 and got poor completion on anything past the third slide, and each one ate a designer's afternoon. They are no longer part of the plan unless the social lead asks for one. Numbered series ("3 of 5") read as content for its own sake, so run a single good post instead.

## Sensitive moments

Check the news before a scheduled card goes out. A cheerful release card next to a public incident in our field looks careless. Hold it and ask. Illustrated flames and fire language are the first things to pull.

## Staff reshares

Staff may reshare cards as they are. Please ask them not to crop the logo or add filters. Sales teams sometimes make their own versions, and we would rather they ask. If you see a home-made card with an old logo or old colors, send it to Brand and leave the person alone. Usually they found an old file in a shared folder.

## Filing

Published cards are saved back to the library with a record. Set `restrictions` if a card carries a dated event or a time-limited statistic, so that nobody reuses it next year.

# Wickhold voice and tone

Noor Eskelund, Head of Brand. Written for the February 2026 rebrand, rewritten in April after the Containment Report went out, last edited in June. Comments go to #brand-review in Slack.

## Start at 3am

Anyone who writes for Wickhold should read an incident channel before writing a line of copy. Kofi Anselm's team keeps a few scrubbed transcripts for new hires. Skip the panic at the top of the thread and find the messages from whoever is running the incident. They tend to look like this:

> 03:14 UTC. A pod in `checkout` started a shell it has no reason to start.
> 03:14 UTC. Wickhold Quenchline froze the process and isolated the pod's network.
> 03:22 UTC. Rest of the namespace is quiet. Still unknown how the shell got there.
> Reading the image history now. Next update 03:45.

That is the voice. It says what happened, what is contained and what is next, in that order, and it stops. It has timestamps where other writers have adjectives. It admits the thing it does not know in the same flat tone as the thing it does. The person writing it is tired and is not going to make their tiredness your problem. Forty people are reading, half of them frightened, and the frightened ones calm down because of how the message is written.

Maren Tolliver and Dov Achterberg were on-call infrastructure leads before they founded this company in Denver in 2019. The voice is theirs by inheritance. The 2026 brand made it official: a wick is the one place a fire is allowed to exist. Production will catch fire in small ways, on ordinary nights, for dull reasons. The mission is to keep small failures from becoming big ones, and the copy should sound like it was written by people who consider that a normal day's work.

## The character

Wickhold is someone who has been paged more often than you have and is not going to bring it up.

**Unhurried.** Nothing in our copy is urgent. A page that hurries the reader is using the same trick as the alert fatigue they came to us to get away from.

**Exact.** "Isolated the pod's network" beats "took action". "220 nodes" beats "at scale". If two engineers would argue over what a sentence means, it isn't finished.

**Unimpressed by itself.** The product is useful. Copy that gasps at it reads as though the writer has not seen it fail. We have seen it fail, and the release notes say so.

**On your side of the pager.** The reader is a peer on the same rota, and we write to them as someone who could take the next shift. No lecturing, no "did you know", no explaining Kubernetes to people who run it.

When the character slips, it usually slips into one of four people:

- **The hero.** Rushes in, saves the day, gets the credit. Early rebrand drafts leaned on firefighters and helmets until Maren pointed out that a firefighter arriving means it already went badly. The customer's on-call team is the competent party in every story we tell.
- **The prophet.** Sees doom everywhere and sells shelter from it. The whole security industry's default register, which makes it invisible to the people we want to reach.
- **The buddy.** "Hey there, Kubernetes friends." Nobody paged at 3am wants a pal.
- **The analyst.** "In today's rapidly evolving threat landscape." Sentences with no one in them. If nothing would change when the paragraph is deleted, delete it.

## What Wickhold believes

These are opinions and we expect some readers to disagree with them. Copy that could have come from any vendor in the category has failed, even if it breaks no rule.

heading_path: Fear is not a sales tool
results.content:
### Fear is not a sales tool

No threat-actor drama. No ticking clocks.

The rule is simple to state and gets broken constantly, because fear copy is the easiest copy in security to write. It covers attackers portrayed as characters with motives and nicknames, anything of the "while you read this" kind, countdowns, "it's only a matter of time", "every second counts", and any sentence that asks the reader to imagine the phone call to the board. Our readers carry a pager. They do not need help imagining it.

Give the same fact without the dread.

Bad: "Attackers are already inside your cluster, and the clock is ticking."

Good: "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]."

The second sentence is more uncomfortable than the first, and it did not raise its voice. Trust the number to do that work.

Breach references have their own rules in the claims document. Read them before you mention one.

### Containment is the whole argument

Something will get through. Every serious engineer already knows this, and the companies who claim otherwise are talking to someone else. Wickhold's position is that the useful question is how far a failure gets and how fast it stops spreading. The whole product line follows from that, and so does most of our vocabulary. If a draft reads as though nothing bad will ever happen to the customer, it's arguing for a different company.

### Say the number, then stop

Claims carry a figure and a source. No adjective stacks.

"Fast" is not a claim. "A fast, powerful, highly scalable runtime platform" is three non-claims in a row. Write the number, say where it came from, and end the sentence. The urge to add a second sentence explaining why the number is impressive is the urge to resist. A reader who needs that sentence is the wrong reader; a reader who doesn't will think less of us for it.

Bad: "Lowmoor Credit Union saw an incredible, game-changing reduction in response times."

Good: "Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes across 220 nodes."

Bad: "Quenchline is extremely lightweight and blazingly quick."

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026."

If there is no figure, there is usually no claim, and the honest move is to describe what the product does in plain mechanical terms. "Isolates a pod's network" needs no number and no source. It's a description. "Industry-leading isolation" needs both and has neither.

### Admit limits

One of the company values, and the one marketing finds hardest. Every product we sell has an edge. Wickhold Evenburn finds drift and exposure paths; it does not contain anything. Quenchline contains what is running; it does not patch the image it came from. Saying so costs a little in the moment and buys a lot of belief for the next claim on the page. Engineers look for the catch. When they find we already named it, they keep reading.

### Specifics outrank concepts

Nobody's bad night was ever improved by a concept. Where a sentence can hold a pod, a node, a policy or a flag, put one in. "Runtime visibility" is a concept. "Which process opened that socket, and when" is something a person wants to know.

## Founder voice and brand voice

There are two voices at Wickhold, and they have one hard line between them.

**Founder voice is first person singular, and it is signed.** Maren writes as "I". Her posts carry her name. She gets to have feelings and doubts, tell a story from a bad night in 2017, and be wrong in public. Dov's technical posts work the same way and are signed "Dov".

**Brand voice never says "I" or "we think".** Website, product pages, company LinkedIn, the company X account, email, decks, reports: no first person singular, ever. "We believe", "we feel" and "in our view" are "we think" in different shoes, and they go too.

**Brand voice uses "Wickhold" or "we" for facts only.** Things that happened, things that are true of the company, things a lawyer could check.

| Fine in brand voice | Not in brand voice |
|---|---|
| We renewed SOC 2 Type II in January 2026. | We think SOC 2 matters. |
| Wickhold serves more than 140 customers. | I've talked to a lot of platform teams. |
| Containment is where incidents are won or lost. | We believe containment is where incidents are won or lost. |

The third row is the useful one. Brand voice still holds opinions. It states them as flat sentences, the way the on-call lead does, and lets the reader disagree. "We think" adds nothing except a hedge.

Practicalities. Nobody else writes as "I" in Wickhold content. Kofi's developer posts and anything from the wider team run in brand voice under a byline, because a byline is credit and a founder post is a person speaking for themselves. Customer quotes are quotes and say whatever was approved. If the content team drafts for Maren, she reads it and changes it before her name goes on, and a post that she has not read does not go out. In the spring a joint Maren-and-Dov byline was tried on one post; "I" became unreadable after two paragraphs, so that was dropped. One author per post.

## Tone by channel

The voice stays the same. How much of it you get changes with the room.

**Landing pages.** The flattest we get. Mechanical, confident, short. The reader is deciding whether to spend ten more minutes, so tell them what the thing does on a cluster and let them go. "Wickhold Quenchline isolates the pod, freezes the process or drains the node, then writes down what it did."

**Blog.** The most room to think. Brand-voice posts walk through how something fails. Dov's posts can argue, and they should. A good post leaves the reader able to do one thing they could not do before, even if they never buy. Avoid the summary paragraph at the end. If the post worked, the reader was there.

**LinkedIn.** The company page is brand voice. Founder posts are where the personality lives. A post runs about 200 words, which suits one story and one point. Write as a person with a job, not a thought leader: no line breaks after every sentence, no "here's what I learned", no lists of lessons from an outage.

**X.** One fact, or one observation, in a dry tone. The account does not chase the news and does not reply to arguments about vendors. It's fine for a post to be plain. "The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is most of a night shift."

**Email.** One person writing to one person who is busy. Say why you are writing in the first sentence. Assume it is being read on a phone in a hallway. No "I hope this finds you well", and since these are brand emails, no "I" at all unless Maren signed it. Customer notices are the exception to everything else in this list and sound like the incident channel at the top of this document.

**Product UI and error text.** The closest thing we have to pure voice. What happened, what state things are in, what to do. "Containment action failed on node `ip-10-2-14-7`: agent unreachable. The pod is still running. Retry or drain the node." Chirpy empty states were tried in 2025 and came out after a customer saw one during a real incident.

**Case studies.** Third person, numbers up front, the customer's team as the subject of most sentences. Enough detail about their environment that a peer recognizes it. A case study that could describe any customer describes none of them.

**The Containment Report.** Annual, every April, and the most formal thing we publish. It reads like a clinical note: findings in flat declaratives, method stated early, no pitch in the body. The product can appear at the end, briefly, once the reader has had what they came for.

**Release notes.** Past tense, specific, no selling. A bug we fixed is described as a bug.

**Press.** Third person, plain, one idea per release. The quote from Maren is the only place with any warmth, and she writes it herself.

**Sales decks and talk tracks.** Same facts, same claims, slightly warmer because a person is in the room. If a slide would embarrass the on-call lead, it comes out.

**Webinars and video.** Script it as speech, then cut a third. Two people talking through a real incident timeline beats one person reading slides. No stock intro music with a heartbeat in it, and no voiceover that sounds like a trailer.

**Support replies.** These are written by the support team and we don't police them, but the same habit applies: repeat what you saw, say what you did, say what happens next. A reply that begins by thanking the customer for their patience has already lost them.

**Events.** Slow Burn Summit in Denver is the one place where we are among friends, and it can sound like that. The stage voice is relaxed and first-name, and the facts on the slides are still the facts. Field Day is smaller and closer to a conversation in a car park. Booth copy is brand voice: short, mechanical, no shouting.

## Tone by audience

Humor depends on the audience, see each persona.

The personas hold the working rules for each reader, including what goes first. What follows is only the register, meaning how the voice sounds once you have chosen your content.

**CISOs.** Level and measured. Assume the reader will forward your paragraph to an audit committee without editing it, and write something they can forward. Risk, time and board language are their native terms: exposure, time to contain, residual risk, ownership. Short sentences, complete ones, no shorthand. Every sentence should survive being read aloud in a room that includes a lawyer.

**Platform engineers.** A good pull-request comment from a colleague you respect. Exact, brief, assumes competence, and shows its working. If there is a YAML snippet that makes the point, the prose can get out of its way. Marketing English reads as noise here and the page will be closed.

**DevSecOps.** These readers sit between the review queue and the pipeline, and they spend their days being the person who says no. Write to someone who is outnumbered: practical, on their side, and specific about what lands in their queue and what stays out of it.

**Compliance leads.** Careful nouns. This reader will notice the difference between "supports" and "meets", and will quote you. Their persona is still being written, so if the piece is aimed mainly at them, ask Noor before guessing.

**Customers mid-incident.** Pure 3am voice. Nothing about the product, nothing about the relationship, no reassurance that isn't backed by a fact. What we see, what we've done, when the next update comes.

**Finance and procurement.** They read a small part of what we write and they read it closely. Plain sentences, the price in the standard form, the terms where they expect them. Anything that sounds like enthusiasm reads to them as a negotiating position.

**Journalists.** Assume no interest in the product and real interest in what is happening to teams. Offer the finding, the method and a person to talk to. Don't send them a story with a hook in it; they have their own.

**Candidates and the community.** Warmer, plainer, and allowed to mention that the work is interesting. The same no-drama rules hold. Nobody here is a rockstar.

## When the news is ours

We will have our own bad days: a bad agent release, a late fix, a false containment that drained a node it should have left alone. The values cover this before anything else does. Say what happened. Contain first. Admit limits. Leave it better for the next on-call.

In practice:

- Lead with what happened to the customer's systems, in their terms.
- Use "we" and an active verb. "We shipped a policy update that drained nodes it should not have." "An issue occurred" is not a sentence we publish.
- Apologize once, plainly, in one short sentence. Then get on with the facts.
- Say what is still unknown.
- Say when the next update comes, and hit that time even if there's nothing new.

Dov signs off anything technical. Priit Salonen reads anything that touches a contract. Nobody in marketing edits the facts for tone.

## One fact, three rooms

The same pair of numbers, set for three readers. The facts stay fixed and the weight moves.

On a landing page, where the reader is deciding whether to keep going:

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

In a note to a CISO, where the number has to fit a conversation about risk:

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Your team's own figure is the one to bring to the risk committee.

In a post for platform engineers, where the first response to a lab figure is suspicion:

> Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026. Your cluster is not our lab. Run it in observe mode and read what it would have done.

None of the three is more honest than the others. Each one hands the reader the number in the form they can use.

heading_path: Subjects that pull the voice off course
results.content:
## Subjects that pull the voice off course

Some topics drag writers back toward the register the rebrand left behind. These are the ones reviewers see most.

**AI agents.** Wickhold Leashgate, in early access, attracts the worst habits in the building, because the whole market is shouting about agents. Treat an agent as a workload with credentials and questionable judgment. Talk about tool calls, agent identity and the blast radius of an agent. Leave the future of work to other people. Anyone who has run production will recognize the problem from there, and that recognition is worth more than any amount of excitement.

**Compliance.** Dull on purpose. Certification status is a fact with one correct wording, and legal owns that wording. Copy the approved sentence and do not improve it. A nicer phrasing here is how a company ends up saying something untrue.

**Money.** Prices are stated flatly, with no "just", "only" or "starting from". Core is $18 per node per month. The reader can decide how they feel about that.

**Company news.** Funding, awards, headcount. Nobody is thrilled, excited or proud. The Series B was $46M in June 2024; that is a date and a number, and the sentence after it should say what changed for customers. If nothing changed for customers, ask whether the post needs to exist.

**Customers.** They did the work. Lowmoor Credit Union's on-call team runs its own incidents, and the product took one job off their list. Avoid "partnered with", "journey" and anything that casts us as the guide who showed them the way.

**Other approaches.** The voice doesn't sneer. Other kinds of product make real trade-offs, and a colleague would describe them as trade-offs: a heavier agent can see more and costs more on the node. Readers respect the writer who can state the other side accurately. Reviewers will cut anything that sounds like a playground.

**Open source.** Kubernetes, eBPF and Helm were here before us. We are users and we say so. Credit the projects, don't imply we invented the kernel feature, and don't describe a community as an "ecosystem we're proud to be part of".

## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

## What sounds like us

| Sounds like Wickhold | Doesn't |
|---|---|
| Here is what happened. | We're reaching out to share an important update. |
| We don't know yet. | We are actively investigating. |
| That part is still yours. | We've got you covered. |
| Start in observe mode. | Begin your containment journey. |
| It took 11 minutes. | In record time. |
| It's a trade-off. | No compromises. |
| The pod is still running. | Your environment remains protected. |

## One rewrite, start to finish

A draft that came through in May, lightly disguised:

> We're excited to announce that we think our powerful new drift capabilities will transform how modern teams approach cloud risk, giving you the confidence you need in an increasingly dangerous world.

The edit went like this.

"We're excited to announce" went first. The reader's interest in our excitement is zero.

"We think" is out, because this is brand voice.

"Powerful", "new" and "modern" were doing nothing. Remove them and the sentence gets more honest and no less informative.

"Increasingly dangerous world" is the fear habit, and it also isn't something we can source.

That left "drift capabilities will transform how teams approach cloud risk", which on inspection means nothing. So the reviewer asked the only useful question: what does a person see on the screen? The product manager's answer became the copy.

> Wickhold Evenburn lists the drift in a cluster and ranks it by exposure path, so the fix order is on one page. It does not contain anything at runtime.

That is shorter, it can be checked, and it names an edge. Nobody involved felt that it was a loss.

## Reading old copy

Pre-2026 material is everywhere: the archive, old decks, the sales team's memory. It sounds different for a reason. The old brand sold watching. It leaned on "always", "every" and "complete", and it got excited in public. A lot of it is competent copy for a company we no longer are.

If you are reusing something from before the rebrand, do not patch the sentences. Take the facts, check that they are still approved, and write it again. Look for these symptoms when reading a draft that someone has recycled: a promise of total coverage, a sentence about seeing with nothing about what happens next, and an excited tone that doesn't match the numbers beside it.

## Tried and dropped

The rebrand ran through a lot of ideas. Recording them saves the next person some time.

- **"3am" as a campaign.** A homepage concept with a live clock counting down to the next page. Striking, and a ticking clock in the literal sense. The 3am idea stayed in this document, which is where it belongs: it's how we write, and readers don't need to be told about it.
- **"Calm" as a stated brand value.** Writing "we stay calm" is not calm.
- **A brand mascot.** A small candle character reached one round of sketches. No one who has been on call wanted it near them.
- **First-person customer stories written as diaries.** Moving, and impossible to get approved. Case studies are third person with numbers.

heading_path: Before you send it for review
results.content:
## Before you send it for review

Read it out loud as a handover to the next on-call. If you stumble, or feel you are selling to a colleague, rewrite that part.

Then a few checks that catch most problems:

- Can a stranger tell what happened, what is contained and what is next?
- Does each claim have a figure and a source, or is it a plain description of what the product does?
- Is there an "I" or "we think" outside a signed founder piece?
- Does anything rely on the reader being scared?
- What's the last line doing there?

Copy review goes through #brand-review, and Noor or one of the brand team turns it around in two working days. Claims go to Priit Salonen's team and take the time the approved claims set. If a deadline leans on either of those, say so early.

# Word list

Everything here applies to anything a customer, prospect, journalist or candidate can read. Slack can say what it likes.

## Banned terms

There are thirteen. They stay out of headlines, body copy, decks, alt text and speaker notes that leave the building. When one shows up in a draft it usually marks the spot where the writer ran out of facts, so deleting it rarely fixes the sentence. Find the fact.

| Term | Why it is out | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| seamless | Putting an eBPF agent on every node has seams: a kernel check, a Helm upgrade, a stretch in observe mode. Platform engineers know this and stop reading when told otherwise. | Say what the rollout takes. |
| robust | Strong against what? The word claims a result and skips the test. | Name the failure the thing survived. |
| leverage | A finance word doing a job that "use" does for free. | Use "use". |
| best-in-class | No class, no judge, no source. It cannot pass "say the number, then stop". | Give the figure and where it came from. |
| next-gen | Every product in this market has been next-gen at some point. The word ages the day it ships. | Say what it does on a node today. |
| single pane of glass | Our readers have been sold this pane many times and own several. It also describes watching, and the job here is containing. | Name the screen and what it shows. |
| holistic | Usually covering for a gap. If something spans cloud and cluster, those two words are shorter and checkable. | List what is covered. |
| unlock | Implies the customer's own work was locked up and we hold the key. Drags padlocks into the room as well. | Say what the reader can now do. |
| empower | The readers already have root. Nobody here hands out power. | Say what changed for them, in a verb they would use. |
| cutting-edge | A claim about us, and an undated one. eBPF is well past being new, and that is one reason it is safe to run in production. | Name the technique. |
| game-changing | An incident is nobody's game, and the claim has no number attached. | Give the before and after. |
| prevent all | A promise no security product can keep. Includes "prevents all", which is the same promise with better grammar. | See the verbs below. |
| stop all | Same promise, same problem. A CISO who reads this line once will discount the rest of the page. | See the verbs below. |

The prose test: if a sentence still reads as true after you swap the product for a toaster, it needed a fact and got an adjective.

## Preferred terms

**Workload, not asset.** Customers run workloads, and that is the word they use in their own runbooks. "Asset" comes from inventory spreadsheets and suggests a thing that sits still. A workload moves, restarts and misbehaves, which is why it needs a runtime product. Inside the marketing team "asset" still means a blog post or an image file; that use never reaches a customer.

**Contain, limit and slow, rather than prevent.** This is the company's argument in three verbs. Something will go wrong on a Tuesday night regardless of what anyone buys. Wickhold Quenchline contains what is already running. Wickhold Evenburn limits exposure. Wickhold Leashgate limits what an agent can reach. "Slow" is the honest verb when the action buys time and does not end the problem. Also keep "eliminate" and "eradicate" out of it; they are "prevent" in a bigger coat.

Use "contain" only when a containment action actually happens. Detection on its own is detection.

One exception came out of a release-notes review. A line saying a patch prevents a crash in the agent is describing our own bug, so it can stay. The rule covers promises about what happens to customers, and a changelog entry makes none.

**Customers, not clients.** Clients have an account manager and a lunch. Customers run our agent in production and page us. A "client" in the software sense stays: `kubectl` is a client, an email client is a client. "Users" is fine when you mean the people logged in to the console, because a customer is the whole company.

heading_path: Not banned, but expect a comment
results.content:
## Not banned, but expect a comment

Reviewers will ask about these. Sometimes the word survives.

- **solution.** Name the product, or say what it does. The word exists to avoid doing either.
- **visibility.** Seeing isn't the job. If the sentence ends at seeing, ask what happens next.
- **real-time.** Fine with a number next to it. Without one it means nothing.
- **AI-powered.** Tells the reader how something was built and nothing about what it does.
- **comprehensive.** Usually untrue, and a reader will go looking for the gap.
- **threat landscape.** A landscape has no one in it. Say which failure you mean.
- **peace of mind.** Nobody on a rota has ever had this.
- **modern.** Compared with what? Say which setup you mean.
- **mission-critical.** To the person on call, everything is.

## Off the list

- **"Platform".** On the first draft in January, then removed. Half our readers are platform engineers.
- **"Blast radius".** Someone proposed banning it as fear language. It stays, because engineers use it flatly and "blast radius of an agent" is how Leashgate work gets scoped.
- **A Slack bot that flagged banned terms.** Tried for a month in the spring. It flagged `client` in every Kubernetes snippet and nobody read its messages after the first week. Removed. Reviewers catch these now.

To add or remove a term, make the case in #brand-review with a real sentence from a real draft. Kofi Anselm's team has a veto on anything engineers actually say.

Noor Eskelund, May 2026

query.query: x governing rules

results.content:
X playbook
==========

Kofi Anselm / DevRel. Written June 2026 when marketing handed the account over to us. Short on purpose.

The audience on X is platform engineers, SREs and the people who maintain the projects we depend on. Nobody on there is shopping. They follow accounts that post useful things and are funny about once a week.

**Length.** An X post from any Wickhold account is 240 characters at most. The platform allows more. We stop at 240 so a post can be quoted with a comment and still read whole, and because anything longer is usually two thoughts. Count the raw text, including the link as typed.

**Who has the password.** DevRel owns the main account. Marketing queues launch posts and report posts; DevRel reviews them. Noor can pull anything at any time. Two-factor is on the shared vault, and nobody posts from a personal phone without it.

**What goes out**

- Release notes in one line, with a link
- Findings from the Containment Report, one figure per post
- Practical tips: an eBPF gotcha, a kubectl one-liner, something odd about containerd
- Clips from Slow Burn Summit talks and Field Day
- CVE notes when a CVE touches something we ship or something our customers run a lot of, with facts and the fix

About three to five posts a week. More during Summit, fewer in December. Nothing goes out just to fill a slot in the calendar.

**What a good post looks like**

One thought. A concrete noun in the first few words. If there is a link, it comes last.

Good:

> Wickhold Quenchline can drain a node for you if your policy says so. It will not write the postmortem.

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].

> Tip: run contain mode on one namespace first. Observe mode tells you what would have happened. Contain mode tells you who in that namespace forgot to mention a sidecar.

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is one whole on-call shift, plus a sandwich.

> Wickhold Evenburn's fix order will not make the list shorter. It will tell you which line to start on.

> Wickhold Leashgate, in early access: tool-call policy for AI agents, with agent identity on every call. It limits what a compromised agent can do. Request access: https://wickhold.example/leashgate

Bad, too long and too many ideas:

> Runtime security is more important than ever as Kubernetes adoption accelerates, which is why we're excited to share that our platform gives teams everything they need across detection, posture and policy, all in one place, and we'd love to show you how it works.

Bad, reads like an ad that wandered onto the timeline:

> Is your cluster safe? Book a demo today and see the difference.

**Threads.** Four posts at most, each one under the same 240 limit, and each one has to stand alone because people will only ever see one. Threads are for walkthroughs: how a pod gets isolated, what shows up in the audit log, what happens when the agent restarts. If a thread wants to be longer, it's a blog post, and the thread links to it.

**Replies.** Answer technical questions fast and link to docs rather than pasting paragraphs. Keep support issues out of public replies: ask for a ticket number and take it to the support queue. Don't argue with anyone about eBPF versus sidecars. It has never once ended well.

**Humor.** Dry, about the work, at our own expense or at the expense of YAML. Never at the expense of a person or a team having a bad day.

**Dropped.** We ran a "Friday failure" series in spring 2026 where engineers sent in their worst outage stories. Good engagement, but it took hours of editing each week to remove anything identifying, so it ended after five rounds. If a Field Day produces a good story and the teller says yes, post it as a one-off.

**Scheduling.** Launch posts are scheduled. Everything else is posted live by whoever is on the DevRel rota, because scheduled tips have a way of going out in the middle of someone else's bad news. If something big is happening in the industry, pause the queue and ask Kofi.

# Wickhold brand guidelines 2026

Noor Eskelund, Head of Brand. Issued February 10, 2026, with the rebrand. Revised September 2026.

These guidelines replace the 2024 guidelines in full. They cover what the brand is, what it stands for and how it looks at the level a writer, designer or marketer needs to make decisions. The detailed working rules for words, claims, channels and images sit in their own documents, and this one does not repeat them.

## 1. What changed in 2026

On February 10, 2026, Wickhold Security became Wickhold. This section records what moved and why, for the people who join after it and wonder how the folder got to look the way it does.

### Why the company rebranded

The 2024 brand made a promise about watching. It suited a company that sold visibility, and it stopped fitting as the product moved on. By 2025 the feature customers talked about in renewals was the moment Wickhold Quenchline isolated a pod's network at 3am and nobody had to get out of bed. Sales calls kept going the same way: the prospect would say every tool they owned could see a problem, and then ask what happens next.

Ilse Varga-Holm, who owns the rebrand, started the work in spring 2025 with a set of about 30 customer and on-call interviews. Maren Tolliver and Dov Achterberg sat in on most of them. The clearest finding was that nobody wanted another thing watching them. They wanted the blast of an incident to be smaller and the morning after to be shorter. That finding drove every decision below.

### What moved

| Element | 2024 | 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Brand name | Wickhold Security | Wickhold |
| Tagline | The 2024 line, now retired | Small fires stay small. |
| Logo | Shield with a flame | Geometric W whose center stroke rises as a wick, tipped by one Ember dot |
| Primary color | Cobalt | Ember |
| Ink | Navy | Soot |
| Ground | White | Tallow |
| Secondary | Sky | Whetstone, Verdigris |
| Type | Inter | Bricolage Grotesque, IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono |

The posture product took a new name, Wickhold Evenburn, on March 2, 2026, three weeks after the company name changed. The two dates were separated on purpose. Customers had one thing to absorb at a time, and the product team needed the extra weeks to change the name in the console.

### How the change rolled out

| Date | What happened |
|---|---|
| Spring 2025 | Interviews begin |
| October 2025 | Name, mark and tagline chosen by the founders, under NDA for most of the company |
| January 2026 | Rebrand teased to customers, with no details |
| February 10, 2026 | Name, logo, tagline, site and these guidelines go live |
| March 2, 2026 | Evenburn name goes live in the console and in customer communications |
| April 14, 2026 | First Containment Report in the new identity |
| Through 2026 | Long tail of old PDFs, deck versions and supplier files |

The transition period is over. Former names are no longer used alongside current ones in new copy. The one standing case for a former name is a historical reference, such as a press archive or a customer who needs to match an old invoice.

### What was tried and dropped

The record is here so that nobody spends a month rediscovering it.

- **Keeping "Security" in the name.** It tested as clear and forgettable. The word was doing the job of a category label, and the boilerplate can do that job in its first sentence.
- **A renamed shield.** The agency's first round kept a shield and took the flame out of it. Customers could not tell it from the vendor logos on their own conference lanyards.
- **A literal candle.** It got a good laugh in the room and looked like a spa.
- **A deep green primary.** Green read as "all clear", which is a promise a security company has no business making with its color. A version of it survived as Verdigris.
- **"Contain first." as the tagline.** It was accurate and it sounded like an order. It lives on as one of the four values.
- **An animated flame in the product.** See the logo section. It is gone.

### Older material

The folder holds a lot of work from before the rebrand. Some of it is useful for reference. None of it is a pattern to copy without checking, and the fact that a document is well made or was recently touched does not make it current.

## 2. Mission

**Keep small failures from becoming big ones.**

The mission is written for the people who run production. A failed deployment, a process that should not be running, a credential in the wrong place: these happen every week in any serious cluster, and they stay dull when somebody contains them early. The company exists to keep them dull.

Three things follow from that wording, and they are the reasons it was chosen.

It accepts that failures happen. A company that claims failures will not happen has stopped talking to engineers. Founders Maren and Dov spent years as on-call infrastructure leads before starting Wickhold in Denver in March 2019, and neither of them has ever met a system that did not fail.

It measures success by size. A contained incident still gets logged, reviewed and fixed. The win is that it stayed at one pod and did not reach the node, or stayed at one node and did not reach the cluster.

It says "keep", which is ongoing work. Containment is something a team does with good tools, every week. The mission gives the product a role in that work and leaves the credit for the outcome with the customer's on-call team.

Use the mission on recruiting pages, in all-hands decks and in the opening of long-form pieces about the company. It is an internal compass first. It should not be pasted on product pages as a slogan, because the tagline already does that job.

A few sentences show the difference between using the mission and hanging it on the wall.

Good, from a recruiting page: "We build software that keeps small failures from becoming big ones. If you have been paged at 3am, you already know why that matters."

Weak: "Our mission is to revolutionize the way the world thinks about failure." It's bigger than the company, and it says nothing an on-call engineer would recognize.

## 3. Values

There are four, and they are written the way an on-call lead would say them.

**Say what happened.**
Report the event in plain order: what occurred, what was affected, what was done, what is next. This applies to incident reports, release notes, customer emails and the company's own mistakes. When a release goes badly, the customer note says so in the first sentence.

Good: "The last Wickhold Quenchline release raised CPU use on nodes running older kernels. A fix shipped on Tuesday. Here is how to check whether you were affected."

Bad: "We're always working to improve performance, and our latest update includes important enhancements."

**Contain first.**
In an incident, limit the damage before explaining it. In marketing, the same ordering applies: the first thing a reader gets is the thing that helps them, and the story of how it came about can wait. The value also sets the company's posture. Wickhold talks about containing, limiting and slowing. A promise of a world with no incidents is a promise no honest vendor can keep.

Good: "At Lowmoor Credit Union, time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes across 220 nodes."

That example gives the result with no adjectives around it and leaves the reader to decide what it means.

**Admit limits.**
Every product has edges, and engineers find them within a week. Naming a limit in advance costs less than having a customer discover it during a bad night, and it makes everything else the company says easier to believe.

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline works at runtime. It does not review code before it ships."

**Leave it better for the next on-call.**
This one comes straight from the founders. When an on-call shift ends, the next person should find the runbook updated, the noisy alert tuned and the handoff note written. Inside marketing it means naming source files sensibly, recording why a decision was made, and putting a correction in the document that was wrong and not only in a thread. It is why the "tried and dropped" list in section 1 exists.

### The values at work

| Value | What it looks like in marketing | What it rules out |
|---|---|---|
| Say what happened | A release note that names the bug | "Various improvements" |
| Contain first | The useful thing in the first line | A long wind-up about the threat landscape |
| Admit limits | A page that says which environments are unsupported | A feature table with a check in every box |
| Leave it better for the next on-call | A source file with a clear name and a note on why | A final deck that only one person can edit |

heading_path: How the values show up in hiring and reviews
results.content:
### How the values show up in hiring and reviews

The values are also used by the people team, so marketing should not rephrase them. Quote them exactly as they appear here, in this order, with the full stop after each one. They are short sentences, so treat them as sentences.
## 4. Positioning

### The brand idea

A wick is where a fire is allowed to exist. It gives the flame a place to be, and it keeps the flame there. That is the idea behind the name, the mark and the tagline. Wickhold accepts that production systems have heat in them. The job is to hold it to a small, known place.

This idea should explain design and copy decisions when a rule doesn't. When two options are both on brand, pick the one that feels calmer and more contained.

### Tagline

The current tagline is **Small fires stay small.**

It is written with sentence case and a full stop, and the full stop is part of it. Do not vary it, translate it into a campaign pun, or extend it with a second clause. It can stand alone under the logo, close a piece, or sit at the end of a deck. It does not need to appear in every piece, and one use per piece is the limit.

The retired 2024 tagline should not appear in anything new, including "then and now" pieces, without a request to Brand.

### Positioning statement

For teams that run Kubernetes in production, Wickhold is the runtime security company that contains failures early. Other tools report what they saw. Wickhold products act on it, within limits the customer's team has set, and tell the team what was done.

This statement is internal. It tells writers where the company stands, and it is not customer copy. The approved public description of the company is the current boilerplate, which is kept and owned separately.

### The market problem

The strongest evidence for this position comes from Wickhold's own research. The Wickhold Containment Report 2026, published April 14, 2026, surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. It found that "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident" and that "the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours" [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].

The gap those numbers describe is between finding something and doing something about it. Detection has become cheap and common. Containment still depends on a person with enough access waking up, reading the alert, deciding, and acting. Wickhold's position lives in those hours.

### Where the category goes wrong

Security marketing has habits that readers have learned to skip. The position is partly defined by not having them.

| Category habit | What Wickhold does |
|---|---|
| Opens with a frightening scenario | Opens with what a team can do about the problem |
| Promises total coverage | Says what is covered and names what is not |
| Sells the dashboard | Shows the containment action and its log entry |
| Treats the on-call engineer as a victim | Treats the on-call engineer as the expert |
| Uses a survey to alarm | Uses a survey to size a problem, then stops |

### Testing a campaign idea

Before a concept goes to design, Ilse's team asks four questions of it.

1. Could any other security vendor run this with their logo on it? If so, it isn't the position.
2. Does it depend on the reader being scared? If so, drop it.
3. Does it show containment, or only talk about it?
4. Would the customer's on-call lead forward it to a colleague without a sarcastic comment?

The "Quiet night" concept from the 2026 launch passed all four, and it became the opening of the launch film: a dark office, one screen, a log line reading that a pod had been isolated, and an engineer who doesn't appear because she is asleep at home.

heading_path: Good and bad expressions of the position
results.content:
### Good and bad expressions of the position

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline can isolate a pod's network the moment a known-bad process starts. Your team sets which actions run on their own."

Good: "Small fires stay small."

Bad: "Total protection for everything you run." This promises what no product can deliver, and it could be anyone's line.

Bad: "Attackers are already inside your cluster. Are you ready?" This is fear, and the question does nothing for the reader.

### How the position developed

The company did not change what it builds. Quenchline has offered detection and containment since September 2020. What changed is which half of that sentence the brand leads with. In the 2024 identity, the watching came first and containment was a feature. In the 2026 identity, containment is the point and detection is what makes it possible. Detection still matters to buyers and should be described accurately. It just isn't the headline.

Evenburn fits the same logic from the other direction. Posture work reduces how much there is to catch fire, and it gives the team a fix order so that the worst exposure path gets closed first. The story to tell is about keeping the fuel down, and it shouldn't be told as a second, separate product category.

Leashgate extends the idea to AI agents, which now take actions inside customers' environments. An agent with broad tools is a new kind of workload that can make a mistake quickly. Leashgate sets out what that agent may do and keeps a record of what it did. It is in early access, and the position should be described with that in mind: a direction the company is working in, with real customers trying it.

### Who it is for
