results.content:
# Visual rules common to every image

Owner: Noor Eskelund, Head of Brand. Last edited September 2026, after the Slow Burn Summit push showed us how many people pick images without opening the metadata.

These rules apply to every image Wickhold publishes: a blog hero, a chart in a white paper, a slide a sales engineer drops into a customer call, a banner at a Field Day. If you are holding an image and wondering whether this page applies, it does.

heading_path: Visual rules common to every image
How the visual rules are layered
results.content:
## How the visual rules are layered

Three layers, read in this order.

1. **This page.** Applies to everything.
2. **The category.** What kind of image is it? Photo, illustration, icon, logo, product screenshot, chart, social graphic, event graphic, legal and trust imagery, anything showing a person.
3. **The content type.** Where is it going? Blog hero, LinkedIn, X, email header, landing page.

Most images touch one rule from each layer, and some touch two categories. A photo of a staff member at a customer site is photography and consent at once, and it has to pass both.

A lower layer can narrow a higher one. The illustration category accepts several formats, for example, and the blog hero page accepts fewer of them. In that case follow the narrower rule for that placement, and the broader rule stays true everywhere else. A lower layer cannot loosen this page. If a content-type page seems to let you do something this page forbids, bring it to Brand, because one of the two pages is wrong and we want to fix it.

Per-campaign exceptions go through Noor's exception log. Without an entry there, if a campaign needs something new, the rule changes for everybody or the campaign changes.

heading_path: Visual rules common to every image
The two rules that come up every week
results.content: ## The two rules that come up every week

heading_path: Visual rules common to every image
The two rules that come up every week
No generated text in any image
results.content:
### No generated text in any image

No image contains text produced by an image model or baked into artwork by a tool that does not treat it as live type. Models misspell product names, invent letterforms and produce near-English that survives one quick look and then gets screenshotted by a customer. We had a test hero in spring where a wall sign read almost like "Quenchline". Nobody caught it until it was in a review deck.

Text in a Wickhold image is set by a person, in the design tool, in the brand typefaces, as a separate layer over finished art. That covers overlays, labels, chart annotations and callouts.

Three things do not count as generated text:

- Words that are really in the scene: a printed rack label, a whiteboard someone wrote on, a door sign. Check that they say nothing embarrassing and name nobody outside the company.
- Real interface text in a true product screenshot.
- The wordmark, which is a vector file, placed by a person.

Some placements allow no overlay at all and others cap it. The content-type page has the number.

heading_path: Visual rules common to every image
The two rules that come up every week
results.content:
### One focal point

Every image has one focal point. A reader should be able to say what the image is of after a second's look. If two things compete, crop or pick another image.

Tests we use in review:

- Squint at it. One shape or area should hold.
- Shrink it to a thumbnail. Something should still be identifiable.
- Describe it in one short sentence without "and". "An engineer reading a terminal in a dark room" passes. "A team at a table and a wall of monitors and a logo on the door" does not.

Collages, split screens and before-and-after pairs fail this unless they are charts, where the comparison is the single point.

heading_path: Visual rules common to every image
results.content:
## Other rules for all images

**Current identity only.** Ember `#C2501F`, Soot `#15181C`, Tallow `#F4EFE6`, with Whetstone `#5E6B73` and Verdigris `#2F8F83` as secondary colors. Bricolage Grotesque, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono for any type on an image. Anything leaning on the 2024 blue palette or the 2024 logo is out, however good it looks. Some of those images are still in the library with no flag on them, so your eye is part of this check.

**No third-party marks.** No real product logos on laptop lids, no cloud provider marks on diagrams, no conference logos in a crop unless the agreement with that organizer allows it. Customer marks are a legal matter and go through Legal first.

**No watermarks,** no preview overlays, no leftover crop marks. If an image arrived with a watermark, its rights are not what you think they are.

**Do not stretch, tint or recolor library files.** Crop freely within the category's limits. Stretching breaks the proportions of the art and recoloring breaks the palette. Filters are out too: the warm look comes from the source image, and a filter laid on a cool image only makes it look cool and filtered. If an image needs a color change to fit, it is the wrong image.

**Export for the placement.** WebP or PNG for web, PNG where transparency matters, SVG for logos and icons when the placement accepts it. Keep web images under 400 KB unless the content-type page says otherwise. JPEG artifacts around Ember shapes are very visible, so check flat illustration at full size after compressing.

**Nothing that frightens.** Images follow the same stance as the copy. Show the small fire or the calm room, and skip the alarm. Red alert screens, countdown timers, sirens and skulls have no place here, even as a joke in an engineering post.

heading_path: Visual rules common to every image
The image library and its metadata
results.content:
## The image library and its metadata

Every approved image lives in the image library, and every image in it has a metadata record. Do not pick from the thumbnail grid and stop there. The thumbnail does not show you the limits on the image.

| Field | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `id`, `filename` | Identity. Filenames were set by different people across several years and tell you little. |
| `type`, `title` | Rough category and a human label. |
| `description` | What is in the picture. Often thin, sometimes empty. |
| `tags` | Search help. Inconsistent, so never treat a missing tag as meaning anything. |
| `usage_rights` | The grant we hold for the file. |
| `restrictions` | The limits on this particular image. See below. |
| `added_date` | When it entered the library, which is not when it was made. |
| `source`, `attribution` | Where it came from. In-house work reads `internal-production`, and `attribution` is usually empty or names the in-house team. Empty attribution means no credit line is needed. |
| `width`, `height` | Pixel size. Check before you plan a crop. |
| `background` | How the image relates to what sits behind it. See below. |
| `safe_on` | Which grounds it can sit on. See below. |
| `variant_of` | Points at the parent when the image is one version of another. |

heading_path: Visual rules common to every image
The image library and its metadata
restrictions: check it before every use
results.content:
### `restrictions`: check it before every use

Read `restrictions` before you use an image, every time, including images you have used before. Restrictions are added after an image enters the library, so last quarter's check does not count.

The field is free text, written by whoever had the reason. There is no fixed vocabulary, so read the sentence instead of searching for a keyword. Three kinds of note turn up in practice:

- **Retirement.** The image is deprecated and must not be used. Some retired files look entirely normal in the grid and carry no other sign. Their tags and titles may even look current.
- **A limited context.** The image may be used in the named context and nowhere else. A note limiting an image to internal use keeps it out of anything a customer, a prospect or the press will see, and that includes sales decks.
- **A person or place.** Something about who or what is shown has changed.

A restriction binds even when the image would be perfect, when a senior person asks for it, and when you found it already published somewhere. If you think one is out of date, ask Brand to change the record. Do not use the image and sort it out later.

An empty `restrictions` field means nobody has recorded a limit. It does not mean the image is on brand. The field is one check among several, and the current-identity rule above still has to pass on your own judgment.

If `restrictions` and `tags` seem to disagree, `restrictions` wins. If `restrictions` and `description` disagree, stop and ask.

heading_path: Visual rules common to every image
The image library and its metadata
results.content:
### `background`

Three values.

- `transparent`: no ground at all. The image takes on whatever is behind it, which is why `safe_on` matters so much for these files.
- `solid`: a flat ground is part of the file, such as a logo on its panel or a hero illustration on Tallow.
- `scene`: the image has its own environment, as every photograph does. You never cut a scene out of its background, and we do not mask people or equipment out of photos.

A file marked `transparent` should be previewed on the actual ground before it ships. A bright fringe can look fine on one ground and show on another.

heading_path: Visual rules common to every image
The image library and its metadata
results.content:
### `safe_on`

Three values, each describing the ground the image is designed to sit on.

- `light`: Tallow and other pale grounds only.
- `dark`: Soot and other deep grounds only.
- `any`: holds up on both.

Treat `safe_on` as a limit, the same way you treat `restrictions`. A `light` image on a dark layout is a defect even if you can still more or less see it. The layout's ground is what matters: a dark band halfway down a light page is a dark ground. When an image sits on a photo, or on Ember or Whetstone, neither word applies directly. Use a `solid` version, or test it and show Brand.

heading_path: Visual rules common to every image
The image library and its metadata
results.content:
### `variant_of`

If the record points to a parent, or other records point at this one, you have siblings. Look at them before you decide the image does not work. The version for your ground often already exists.

heading_path: Visual rules common to every image
results.content:
## Picking an image: the order

1. Decide the category and read that page.
2. Decide the content type and read that page.
3. Search the library. Search by description and by a few different words, since tags are uneven.
4. Open the record. Read `restrictions` and `usage_rights` first, then `background`, `safe_on` and size.
5. Look at the picture itself at full size against the current identity. Metadata does not catch everything.
6. Check it against the rest of the layout, on the real ground.
7. Add it to the draft with its `id` noted in the review comment, so Brand can trace it.

heading_path: Visual rules common to every image
results.content:
## Three picks, worked through

**A blog post on draining nodes before an upgrade.** The writer finds a warm photo of a rack door. The title and tags look right and `restrictions` is empty. At full size, the photo is clean and it passes. It needs a crop, so the writer checks `width` and `height` first and confirms the focal point stays in frame.

**A dark section on a pricing comparison page.** The designer drops in a spot illustration that looked good on the last page. The record says `background: transparent` and `safe_on: light`, so it fails on this band. The record has no `variant_of`, but another record points at it as a parent, and that sibling is `safe_on: dark`. Problem solved in two minutes.

**A customer webinar invitation.** The perfect team photo has a line in `restrictions` that the writer almost skipped, because the thumbnail looked fine and the image had been used on the website last year. The line changes the answer. The image stays out, whatever last year's page did, and the writer picks again.

heading_path: Visual rules common to every image
results.content:
## Asking for something new

If the library has nothing suitable, do not borrow from the web, do not pull an image from a past deck, and do not take it from a teammate's desktop. Files outside the library have no record and nobody can check their rights.

Requests go to the brand designers through the design queue with the placement, the deadline and one sentence on what the image should show. Allow five working days for illustration and more for photography that needs a shoot. Anything made for you gets a metadata record before it ships.

heading_path: Visual rules common to every image
results.content:
## Review

Brand reviews every new image and every first use of a library image in paid, press and homepage work. Anything else can ship on the owner's own check against this page, and Brand samples it monthly. Pull anything that fails the sample, even if it has already gone out.

Legal review is separate. It looks at claims, customer marks and consent. A pass from Legal is not a pass from Brand, and the other way around.

# Image accessibility

Web lead's notes, cleaned up by Brand in May 2026 after the customer procurement questionnaire asked us about this and we had no document to point to.

## Alt text on every image

Every image has alt text. This covers blog images, email images, landing pages, social uploads where the platform offers the field, and images in PDFs. The author of the piece writes it, because the designer usually does not know why the image is there.

Write what the reader would lose if the image failed to load. One or two plain sentences, under about 125 characters when you can manage it. Skip "image of" and "picture of". Do not stuff keywords. Do not paste the `description` field from the library: that describes the file, and alt text describes what the image is doing in this piece.

| Image | Bad | Good |
|---|---|---|
| Photo | "Engineer, Kubernetes, security, on-call, data center" | "An engineer reads a terminal in a dim equipment room." |
| Product screenshot | "Screenshot of dashboard" | "Quenchline shows one pod isolated, with network access removed and the process frozen." |
| Chart | "Bar chart" | "Median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours. Wickhold Containment Report 2026." |
| Logo | "logo.png" | "Wickhold logo" |
| Illustration | "Decorative graphic" | "A cut-paper wick with a single small Ember flame." |

Charts and screenshots carry the finding in the alt text, and the reader should not need the picture to get the number. If the chart has more than about four values, put the values in a table or the body copy under it and let the alt text state the point.

Any text set on an image must also appear in the alt text or the surrounding copy. Screen readers cannot read a stat card.

The "every image" part holds for decorative images too. If an image truly adds nothing, the first question is why it is in the piece. Background textures set in CSS are not images for this purpose and need no alt.

## Contrast: 4.5:1 for text

Text on any image or graphic meets at least 4.5:1 against what is directly behind it. We apply the same floor to all sizes, including large headlines. A designer will point out that the web standard relaxes for large type. We know. The single number is easier to check, and a stat card shrinks to thumbnail size in a feed, where large type stops being large. This floor governs images. Layouts follow the logo and color addendum.

Measured ratios for the palette:

| Pair | Ratio | Text allowed? |
|---|---|---|
| Soot on Tallow | 15.5:1 | Yes |
| Tallow on Soot | 15.5:1 | Yes |
| Whetstone on Tallow | 4.8:1 | Yes |
| Verdigris on Soot | 4.5:1 | Yes, just. Test your export |
| Ember on Tallow | 4.1:1 | No |
| Soot on Ember | 3.8:1 | No |
| Ember on Soot | 3.8:1 | No |
| Tallow on Ember | 4.1:1 | No |
| Verdigris on Tallow | 3.4:1 | No |
| Whetstone on Soot | 3.2:1 | No |

This surprises people: Ember does not carry text on our grounds, and no text sits on Ember in an image. Ember is for shapes, rules and the focal element. Headlines on Tallow are Soot. Headlines on Soot are Tallow.

Over a photo, measure against the lightest spot behind the letters for Tallow text and the darkest spot for Soot text. An even-looking dark photo often has one bright lamp right under the word. If the text fails anywhere, put it on a solid Soot or Tallow panel. Do not add a gradient scrim: our illustration and graphic language has no gradients, and scrims tend to fail at their edges anyway.

## Color alone

Do not use color as the only signal. Ember and Verdigris are close in lightness and can merge for a reader with red-green color blindness. Label things directly.

## Motion

Looping GIFs stop after three loops, or ship as static. Nothing flashes more than three times a second. A product demo clip on a landing page has a pause control and does not autoplay with sound.

## Checks before publishing

- Alt text present and written for this placement
- Text on image measured, with the worst spot checked
- Image still makes sense at 320px wide
- Meaning does not depend on color alone

# Blog hero images

Content team working rules, June 2026.

**Every blog post has one hero. It is a 16:9 illustration or photo. It is never a dashboard.**

Product UI in the hero looks like an ad on top of an article, and the detail goes illegible at the size most people see it, which is the preview card. If a post is about a product screen, put the screenshot in the body, at a size where it can be read.

## Narrower than the category pages

Not everything in the illustration category qualifies here:

- **Hero illustrations only.** A spot illustration is transparent and square, and it sits inside body copy. Set as a hero, it leaves a small object floating in a wide band, so it is out.
- **No abstract backgrounds.** They have no focal point on their own, and a hero has no type set over it.
- **Tallow or Soot, matched to the post.** Illustration category rules allow either. For blog heroes, default to Tallow. Use Soot for incident retrospectives and long technical posts, so that the list page has some rhythm.

And from photography:

- **Landscape only.** Portrait photos in the library cannot become 16:9 without losing most of the frame.
- **A person is allowed as the subject, but the post has to be about the work** and not a staff profile.

No text on the hero at all, including the post title. The blog template sets the title in live type below the image. Older posts had titles burned into the image, and they looked wrong in every preview card that also printed the title.

## Size and crop

Export at 1600x900. Most library heroes and photos are 3:2, so you will lose some height. Crop from the top and bottom, then check that the focal point has survived. A hero illustration's focal element usually sits off center and the quiet part can go. Some platforms crop preview cards further, so keep the focal point out of the outer tenth of the frame.

Do not upscale. A 1536-wide source enlarged to 1600 is about the limit, and it should look clean at full size.

## Choosing by post type

| Post | Hero |
|---|---|
| Founder essay, signed by Maren | Photo of a working room, or a quiet illustration |
| Technical post by Dov or the engineering team | Infrastructure photo or a concept illustration tied to the mechanism |
| Customer story | Photo from that customer's site if released, otherwise an illustration. Never a stand-in photo that implies it is their site |
| Containment Report findings | Illustration. Save the charts for the body |
| Comparison post | Neutral illustration. No competitor logos or product screens |
| Incident analysis or a post about a breach | Quiet illustration without flame, or an empty-room photo. Keep it plain |

The hero is chosen for the idea in the post. A post on default containment policies should not get a generic "engineer with laptop". Find the one object that matches: a tray under a wick, a closed rack door, a hand on a breaker.

## Avoiding repeats

Check the last ten posts on the blog before you commit. The same image twice in a month makes the blog look thin, and readers on the index page see them side by side. Since a hero image goes out in the social card by default, check the record's `restrictions` as you would for social use.

## Open graph card

The hero doubles as the social preview card unless a separate card is uploaded. Look at the preview before publishing, as the crop differs from the page. If the preview loses the focal point, upload a separate crop.

## Series and guest posts

A multi-part series uses one hero object across all its parts, changed slightly each time. Guest posts from customers follow the same rules, and a guest's own company image only runs if Brand has checked it. Never accept a stock image from a contributor.

## Credit and caption

No caption on heroes. No credit line unless the record's `attribution` calls for one.

## Who picks

The post's author proposes and the blog editor approves. The first use of a new hero in a homepage feature goes through Brand review.

# Email header images

From the lifecycle marketing manager, March-May 2026 tests, tidied in June.

## Spec

**600px wide. No text in the image.**

The file itself is 600px wide. We tried a 1200px source scaled down in the HTML, and a couple of older desktop mail apps rendered it at full width and broke the layout. So: exactly 600, height between 150 and 240, under 150 KB.

No text means none, and it is stricter than other placements that allow overlay set in design. A large share of readers load email with images off, and headers get blocked first. If the headline is in the picture, those readers get an empty box. Headlines, dates and CTAs go in live HTML. A header image that says "Slow Burn Summit" in type is out, even when a designer set it properly and even if the art is otherwise approved. Put the event name in the first line of the HTML.

That also rules out the social templates, which all carry type, and charts, which need labels.

## What to use

- A hero illustration crop, on Tallow, with one Ember focal element in the center third
- A photo crop with a calm, simple subject

600 wide by 200 tall is a thin strip from a 3:2 source. Pick images whose focal point fits in a band, such as a row of tiles or a cable tray. A person's face at this crop rarely works, because it either fills the strip or gets cut off.

## Transparency and dark mode

Do not use transparent PNGs in email headers. Spot illustrations and other `background: transparent` files are out here, whatever their `safe_on` says. Several mail apps darken the message in dark mode, and they do it unevenly: some swap the ground and leave images alone, and some invert parts of both. A flat ground inside the image keeps the header predictable. Always send a `solid` or `scene` image.

The wordmark sits in its own table cell above the header image, as a panel variant, with alt text. Do not bake the logo into the header picture, since the header is blocked more often than a small logo and you lose the sender's identity with it.

## When to skip the header

Plain-text style emails from Maren or Dov have no header image at all, because an image makes them look like a campaign. The same goes for service notices about incidents or maintenance. Reserve headers for newsletters, event invitations and report announcements.

## By email type

| Email | Header |
|---|---|
| Monthly newsletter | One hero illustration crop, changed each issue |
| Report announcement | Illustration taken from the report cover art, with its title removed |
| Event invitation | Photo crop or illustration, cleared for event use |
| Product update | Usually none. A small product crop in the body does more |
| Sales follow-up | None |
| Renewal or billing notice | None |

Do not animate headers. Some mail apps only show the first frame, which then has to work alone. Do not slice a header into several image cells. That technique causes hairline gaps in the same older apps that dislike large images.

Keep one crop per campaign and reuse it across the sequence, so that the second and third sends read as a set. Each one still gets its image record checked, because `restrictions` can change between sends.

## Before sending

Send a test to the seed list. Check with images off, and in dark mode on a phone. The email should read completely with the header missing.

# Landing page imagery

Web team and Brand, last updated September 2026.

## The hero

**A landing page hero shows product UI or a working room.** Those two options only.

That excludes illustration from the hero slot, even though we use it heavily elsewhere. Visitors on a landing page are deciding whether Wickhold is real. A screen from the product, or a real room where this work happens, answers that faster than a metaphor.

Use product UI when the page is about a product or a capability. Use a working room when the page speaks to a role or a problem and there is no single screen to show.

| Page | Hero |
|---|---|
| Quenchline product page | Product UI: one containment action |
| Evenburn product page | Product UI: exposure path or fix order |
| Leashgate early access page | Product UI: a tool-call policy, with the early access pill in frame |
| Platform engineering solutions page | Working room, or a terminal-adjacent product view |
| CISO or board-facing page | Working room. No people posing |
| Campaign page for the Containment Report | Working room |
| Event registration | A working session photographed at a past Slow Burn Summit, cleared for this use |

## Narrower than the screenshot rules

Product screenshots in general may show a full frame or a crop. In a landing hero:

- **A crop only.** No full-dashboard views. The hero width on a laptop leaves about 700px for the image, and a 1600x1000 frame shrinks to illegible at that size
- **One callout at most.** Up to three are allowed elsewhere
- **A mobile check.** At 390px wide the crop has to show something readable. If it cannot, supply a tighter mobile crop

For working rooms, narrower than photography:

- **No visible screens with content,** so that the eye goes to the headline
- **The photo has to work with the headline beside it.** Type does not sit over the room. The layout is split, or the image sits below

## Legal pages carry no people

Terms, privacy, subprocessors, the DPA page, and the like: no people in any image on these pages. That covers portraits, illustrated silhouettes, hands in a shot and a team in the footer strip. The same applies to the legal section of any combined page.

## Further down the page

Sections below the hero have more room. Spot illustrations work in feature rows. Check each section's ground, since landing pages usually alternate Tallow and Soot bands, and a `safe_on: light` file dropped in a Soot band disappears. Nav and footer logos need checking band by band as well.

Screenshots in the body can run larger and carry callouts. Keep one image per section at most.

Customer logo strips: only what Legal has approved, and no more than the approved set, even when a strip looks empty. Keep them in one tone. Do not recolor logos in Ember.

Quote portraits go through the people and consent check first.

## Performance

Hero image under 250 KB on the wire. Serve WebP with sizes set, and do not lazy-load the hero. SVG for logos and icons. Everything below the fold lazy-loads. A slow page is a credibility problem for a company that sells to platform engineers, and they will open dev tools.

## Video in a hero

Allowed: a silent loop of a containment action, under ten seconds, with a poster frame that passes the hero rule by itself. Not allowed: a talking-head brand film. We tried one on the old homepage and the bounce numbers were bad enough to end the debate.

## Reuse across pages

A/B test variants use the same hero rule. If you test a hero, both arms must pass. An illustration "just for the test" still fails, and test pages have a way of becoming permanent.

Do not use the same working-room photo on two product pages. Visitors move between them, and a repeated picture makes the site look small.

## Common hero rejections

| Submitted | Problem |
|---|---|
| Illustration of a wick on the Quenchline page | Good art, wrong slot. Move it to a feature row |
| Full incident page, shrunk | Illegible. Crop to the one action |
| Bright stock-looking meeting room | Fails the working-room test, and it could be any company |
| Product UI floating on a laptop mockup | Adds a second object. Use the crop alone |
| Abstract background with a headline | No product and no room, so it answers nothing |

## Open graph and paid variants

Each page needs its own preview image, built from the hero crop. A preview with a product crop needs a larger, simpler view of the same action. Paid campaign pages should reuse the same hero as the ad, so that the click feels continuous.

Region-specific pages use the same imagery unless Legal says otherwise. Do not localize by swapping in a landmark photo.

## Review

Every landing page hero is a first use for that page and goes through Brand. Paid landing pages also go to Legal for the claims on the page, and the image goes along with them, because a screenshot can make a claim too.

Allow two working days for Brand. Campaign deadlines are not exempt, so book it when the page is scoped.

# LinkedIn images

Social lead's notes, updated August 2026.

## The spec

- **1200x627.** Export at exactly this size. Anything else gets cropped by the platform, and the crop rarely helps
- **At most seven words of overlay text**
- **Overlay text is added in design**, as live type in the template, over a finished image

Seven words means seven, counted the plain way. A hyphenated word is one word, and a number is one word. The logo does not count. A source line does count, so most stat images move the source into the post copy, which is where we want it anyway.

The seven-word cap narrows what the social graphics rules allow. A stat card on any other surface can carry a measure line and a source. On LinkedIn it gets the number and the short label only.

| Overlay | Words | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Small fires stay small. | 4 | Good |
| Median time to contain: 7.4 hours | 6 | Good, source in the post |
| 11 minutes, down from 4 hours | 6 | Good, with Lowmoor named in the post |
| Contain first. Then find out what happened. | 7 | Good |
| What Wickhold learned from surveying 412 platform and security leaders | 10 | Too long |
| Is your team ready for a runtime incident? | 8 | Too long, and it is a question |

## What goes in the frame

Use, in rough order of how well they have done for us:

1. A photo of real work, with no overlay at all
2. A stat card from the social templates. Quote cards rarely fit the cap
3. A short product crop showing one action, large enough to read in the feed
4. A hero illustration, cropped

Library images are 3:2, so a 1200x627 crop loses about a fifth of the height. Keep the focal point near the vertical center. Spot illustrations should sit on a solid Tallow or Soot layout from the template. They are transparent and LinkedIn will show them on its own background if you upload them as they are.

Do not run overlay text across a photo's focal point. Text goes on a solid band or in the quiet side of the frame.

## By account

**Company page.** Follows all of the above. Logo present on designed images, absent on plain photos.

**Founder accounts.** Maren's and Dov's posts take a plain photo or no image. Designed cards with a company logo look like an ad under a personal post, so skip them. No overlay text on founder images unless Maren asks for it.

**Staff.** Anyone can use the approved templates. Reshare the file as it is.

## Document posts and video

PDF document posts are off the plan, for the same reasons as carousels. Native video follows the screenshot rules for captures. A title frame counts as an image and falls under the seven-word cap.

## Timing against the event calendar

Dated images age badly. A card that names a date comes down from the scheduled queue the moment the date moves. After the event, do not reuse it. Set `restrictions` on the record when you file it, as with any time-limited card.

## Series that have worked

Monthly "from the Containment Report" posts with one number and no other decoration. Plain photos in Field Day recaps, chosen with the people rules in mind. Short "what changed in this release" crops. What has not worked: anything that looks like a slide. If a LinkedIn image looks as if it came from a deck, redo it.

## Checks

- 1200x627 exactly
- Count the words
- Overlay legible at phone width
- Image record read, including `restrictions`

The picture should still make sense with the post text collapsed, since the image is often all a reader sees before "see more".

The most common error in the last quarter was a logo dropped on without checking the ground. The second was a stat shortened until it no longer said what the source said. If shortening changes the meaning, use a different stat or use no overlay.

# X images

An image on X is optional. Most of our best posts have none. Add one only when it shows something the words cannot: a chart, a config snippet, a piece of the product doing its job.

**Never a stock photo.** Nothing bought or licensed, and nothing from the library that could pass for one. X is where our engineering audience spends its time, and a generic office shot under a technical post costs us credibility in that thread. A photo from the library is allowed only if it shows something real and specific, such as a rack or a cable run we can name.

## What works

- A code or YAML card on Soot, from the engineering post format
- A tight product crop of one containment action
- One chart with its title
- A spot illustration, flattened on Tallow or Soot, for a light post

This is narrower than the social graphics rules in two ways. No overlay text on photos here, since the feed crop is unpredictable. And no quote cards: on X, type the quote into the post with the customer's name.

## Size

16:9, 1600x900. Keep the focal point in the middle, as the timeline crops and phone previews trim the edges. Long screenshots of text get a "show more" crop, so do not post them. Write a thread.

heading_path: Crops and overlays, good and bad
results.content:
## Crops and overlays, good and bad

Good: a 40-line policy file cut down to the eight lines that matter, in IBM Plex Mono on Soot.

Good: one bar chart from the Containment Report, with its title readable at phone width and the source in the post.

Bad: a LinkedIn card reposted as it stands. X crops the bottom edge off, which is where the logo sits. A bad image is worse than no image here, so when an image needs a third round of fixes, drop it and post the text alone.

Product posts about Leashgate deserve an extra look, since a tight crop can lose the early access pill. Keep it in frame or pick a different crop.

## Replies and threads

One image per post at most, and no images in replies to strangers. In a thread, only the first post needs one, if any. Do not attach a marketing card when replying to someone who raised a problem in public.

Memes and reaction images: no. Most use third-party material, and the voice doesn't need them.

Kofi's team can post without a Brand review if the image passes the common checks. Company account images go through the social lead.

# Data visualization

Charts are built from data by a person, in code or the design tool. They are never drawn by an image model and never traced from somebody else's report. Written for the 2026 Containment Report and kept for everything since.

## What a chart is for

A Wickhold chart makes one point. Write the point as the title, in a full sentence, in sentence case. The chart then shows why that sentence is true.

| Bad title | Good title |
|---|---|
| Time to contain by team size | Median time to contain is 7.4 hours |
| Survey results | 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident |
| Lowmoor Credit Union performance | Lowmoor's time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes |

If you cannot write the sentence, you do not have a chart yet. You have a table, and a table is often the better choice. Engineers like tables. For fewer than three numbers, set the number in type and skip the chart.

## Data you can chart

Only approved figures go into public charts. A chart does not launder a number: the rules on claims, ages of statistics and lab figures apply to the chart the same way they apply to a sentence.

- Survey data carries its report name and year, and the sample where there is space. The 2026 report surveyed 412 platform and security leaders.
- Customer results appear only with approved customers, with node counts: Lowmoor at 220 nodes, Ostler at 1,900 nodes.
- A lab figure keeps its label on the chart itself: "in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026". Do not move it to a footnote on another page.

No invented or "illustrative" numbers in published charts, even on an unlabeled axis. A rising line with no scale is a claim with nothing behind it.

Every chart carries a source line at the bottom, in the citation format from the style guide, small and in Whetstone on Tallow.

## Color

Bars and lines use the palette.

- **Ember for the one series or bar that makes the point.** All others are Whetstone.
- On Soot, use Tallow for context series, with Ember as the highlight. Whetstone is too dim to read there.
- Verdigris is the second highlight, used only when two series truly need names, such as before and after.
- No Ember tints. If you need a ramp for ordered data, use Soot to Whetstone to pale Tallow steps.

Ember, Whetstone and Verdigris sit very close together in lightness. Printed in grayscale, or viewed by a reader with color blindness, they merge. So hue never works alone: label each series directly on the line or bar, and separate adjacent bars with a gap. Legends are a last resort, since they send the reader back and forth.

Red and green are not used for bad and good. A chart about containment should not look like a stock ticker or an alert console.

## Form

- Horizontal bars for comparing named things, since labels fit
- Lines for change over time, with no more than four lines
- A single before-and-after pair for customer results
- Bars start at zero. Always. Line charts may start elsewhere, with a labeled axis and a reason
- Time axes use real intervals. Do not compress the gap between 4 hours and 11 minutes with a broken axis to make the chart prettier. The small bar is the story

Not used: pie charts, doughnuts, gauges, radar charts, 3D anything, dual axes, stacked areas with more than three bands, bubble charts, Sankey diagrams in marketing, and world maps with glowing dots. We tried a Sankey in the Containment Report draft to show incident paths. It took a paragraph to explain and everyone hated it.

## Type and labels

Chart titles in Bricolage Grotesque. Axis labels and data labels in IBM Plex Sans. Commands and metric names, where they appear, in IBM Plex Mono.

Label units every time, and spell out units in axis titles ("hours to contain"). Round to the precision of the source: 7.4 hours stays 7.4, and it does not become "about 7" or "7.40".

Gridlines are thin, Whetstone at a low weight, and only where they help a reader estimate a value. If each bar has a data label, delete the gridlines and the axis.

## Diagrams

Architecture diagrams fall under this page. Boxes are flat, with a 1.5px Soot stroke or a solid Tallow fill on Soot. Arrows are straight or right-angled, and each one is labeled with what actually passes along it. The eBPF agent, the node, the pod and the control plane are drawn the same way each time. One Ember element marks the part the diagram is about. No cloud vendor icons, and no clouds drawn as clouds. A diagram with more than about nine boxes should be split into two.

## Grounds and export

Charts go on Tallow or Soot, the same as illustrations. Keep an editable source file and record where it lives in the `description` field of the library record. Export PNG at twice the display size, or SVG for the web if the page supports it. Charts that will sit on either ground are exported twice, and the second file gets `variant_of` pointing at the first.

## Tables

When a table is the right call, keep it plain: horizontal rules only, Soot text on Tallow, numbers right-aligned in IBM Plex Mono so that digits line up. Highlight one row with an Ember rule at its left edge. Do not zebra-stripe.

## Good and bad chart notes

**Good annotation:** "Teams with a default containment policy" with a short rule pointing at one bar.

**Bad annotation:** "Shocking gap!" Or any wording that treats a survey number as a threat. The numbers carry enough on their own.

**Good source line:** the report name, the year and a link, formatted as the style guide asks.

**Bad source line:** "Source: industry research."

## Review

Data checked by whoever owns the source: product marketing for the Containment Report, Legal for customer results. Brand checks form and color. Do not skip the first of these because the chart "only reuses" a number from an earlier piece.

owner: Brand design
reviewed: 2026-06-18

# Illustration

Everything we draw looks like it was cut from paper and laid on a table. That style came out of the rebrand work, and it is deliberately easy to recognize at a small size next to a competitor's glowing network diagram.

## The style

**Flat cut-paper shapes.** Crisp edges with a slight hand-cut irregularity. Layers can overlap. Depth comes from stacking, and the only shadow allowed is a hard offset shape in one flat, darker tone.

**One Ember focal element.** Exactly one thing in the picture is Ember. That is where the eye goes. Everything else is Soot, Tallow, or a small amount of Whetstone or Verdigris.

**On Tallow or Soot.** Those are the only two grounds for finished illustration. An Ember ground removes the focal element, because nothing can stand out from it. Whetstone and Verdigris grounds look muddy.

**No gradients.** None, anywhere: no soft shadows, glows, blurs, mesh fills or textured airbrush. If a shape needs to look lit, cut a second shape. In review, this is the rule most often broken by accident, usually by a shadow effect left on by default in the design tool or by an export that adds banding.

Also out: outlines around shapes, 3D, isometric projection, photographic textures pasted on shapes, and stock vector packs. We tried isometric cluster diagrams in January. They looked like every infrastructure startup's site, and they required a depth that flat paper cannot give.

## What to draw

The brand idea is a wick: the place where a fire is allowed to exist. Use that vocabulary and its everyday relatives.

| Idea | Shapes that work |
|---|---|
| Containment | A ring around a small flame, a tray, a snuffer held above a wick, a firebreak cut through paper grass |
| Isolation of a workload | One tile lifted out of a grid, a pod shape with a paper band around it |
| Posture and drift (Evenburn) | A row of even flames with one leaning, a level, a line of tiles slightly out of true |
| Tool-call policy (Leashgate) | A short tether, a gate latch, a loop of cord around a post |
| On-call | A lamp and a mug, a single lit window in a dark paper building |
| Fix order | Steps cut from paper, three stones across a stream |

Keep the flame small. A small flame contained is the entire idea, and a large one means disaster, so the flame should stay well under a tenth of the frame. If the concept seems to need a wall of fire, the concept is wrong.

Kubernetes has its own visual habit of hexagons and ship wheels. Do not draw the Kubernetes logo, which is someone else's mark. Pods are tiles. Nodes are trays or shelves. Clusters are groups of those on a shared ground.

## People in illustrations

Rarely. When a figure is needed, show a simple paper silhouette with no face, working at something. Do not use characters, mascots or recurring cartoon engineers. We had a proposed mascot in the rebrand round, a little candle with eyes, and we all agreed to pretend it never happened.

## Formats in the library

| Format | Size | `background` | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hero illustration | 1536x1024 | `solid` | Wide placements, full scene with ground included |
| Spot illustration | 1024x1024 | `transparent` | Inline in body copy, feature grids, beside text |
| Abstract background | 1536x1024 | `solid` | Behind type in designed layouts. No focal element |

Hero illustrations already contain their ground. Check whether the file is the Tallow or the Soot version and place it in a section where it does not produce a visible box edge against a slightly different ground. Sample the color: if the layout ground is exactly Tallow or Soot, the edge disappears, which is what you want.

Spot illustrations take on whatever sits behind them, so `safe_on` matters. Many spots use Soot shapes and are `safe_on: light`, and those shapes vanish on a dark layout, leaving a floating Ember fragment. Others are built for dark and carry Tallow shapes. Check the record, look at `variant_of` for a sibling, and preview on the real ground. If an image is `any`, still look for a pale fringe along cut edges on Soot.

Do not put a spot illustration on a photograph. Do not put a spot on an Ember band. Do not put a box behind a spot to make it safe on the wrong ground, because the box will look like a mistake. Use the correct version or ask for one.

Abstract backgrounds exist to carry type. On their own they have no focal point, so they are never published without the layout on top of them.

## Composition

- Hero: focal element off center, with at least a third of the frame quiet. That quiet space is where crops happen.
- Spot: centered, with an even margin. No shape touches the edge of the canvas.
- Scale: one size jump between focal element and supporting shapes. Eleven small shapes around one medium shape reads as confetti.
- Fewer shapes than you think. Most good spots have under eight pieces of paper.

## Color limits

Ember appears once, as a single element. Two separated Ember shapes means two focal points. If the composition needs a second accent, use Verdigris, and keep it small. Whetstone is good for the supporting middle layers on Tallow, although its value is close to Ember's, so it does not provide much separation when placed directly next to the focal element. Leave a Soot or Tallow gap between them.

All colors are exact palette values. Do not use tints of Ember. Tints turn it toward pink and off brand.

## Series

When a piece needs several illustrations, such as a report with chapter openers, vary the object and keep the ground, scale and Ember position consistent. Mixing Tallow and Soot grounds within one piece is fine only if it follows the document's structure, for example one dark chapter opener per part.

## Report covers and chapter openers

Long pieces earn one larger concept. The Containment Report cover uses one cut-paper object at a large scale on Soot, with the title set as live type by a designer. Chapter openers repeat that object in a changed state, for instance the tray filling up or a wick burned further down. This gives a long PDF a thread through it without any extra Ember.

## Concepts that failed in review

| Concept | Why it failed |
|---|---|
| Paper flame in a glass jar | Reads as a candle ad, and the jar needed a highlight, which needs a gradient |
| A fire engine | Cute, and it suggests rescue after the damage is done |
| A forest fire with one saved tree | Too much fire, plus sentimental |
| A dog on a leash for Leashgate | Everyone laughed, then nobody could explain the agent. The tether alone works |
| A map of connected glowing nodes | Off style, and it looks like every other vendor |

## Export checklist

PNG for transparent files, with a real alpha channel. Open the file on Tallow and on Soot, then zoom to 200% on the cut edges. Check that the Ember value samples at `#C2501F`, since color profiles in some export paths move it slightly. Save the editable vector source beside the export and record where it lives.

## Requests and review

Give the designer the idea in one sentence and the placement. Do not sketch the metaphor yourself in the request unless you are sure of it: people usually ask for a shield, and we do not draw those. New illustrations get a review at thumbnail size and at full size on both grounds. Once approved, the file enters the library with a complete record, including `background`, `safe_on` and `variant_of` for any ground-specific sibling.

Good request: "Blog post about draining a node before an upgrade. Calm, procedural."

Bad request: "Something cool and techy with flames and a shield for our big launch!!"

# Photography

Brand team, revised July 2026. The look was set for the rebrand and has not changed. What changed this summer is the section on judging library photos by eye, because we kept seeing the same bad picks in drafts.

## The look

Wickhold photography looks like it was taken by someone who was already in the room.

**Available light.** Windows, overhead tubes, the glow of a laptop, a desk lamp. No strobes, ring lights or colored gels. If a room is too dark for the shot, use a longer exposure or find a better room.

**Warm and slightly underexposed.** Think of the last hour of a working day. Skin tones stay warm and natural. Shadows may go deep, though they should not go black across half the frame. If the image histogram crowds the right side, it is too bright for us.

**Working rooms and real infrastructure.** Equipment rooms, cable trays, network closets, a shared office with coffee rings on the table, a laptop open at a kitchen counter during an on-call shift. Places where the work of running Kubernetes actually happens. The subject of a security company's photo library is the people on call and the things they keep running.

**Honest mess.** Leave the cables. Leave the sticky notes (after reading them). A tidied room reads as staged, and staged reads as an advertisement.

## Subjects we want more of

- Hands on a keyboard, shot from the side, with screens angled away or dark
- Two people talking through a problem at a whiteboard, mid-sentence
- Rack doors, patch panels, labeled cable runs, in warm light
- A notebook with a hand-drawn cluster diagram
- A small team around one laptop late in the day
- The Denver office at the end of the afternoon
- Customer-side infrastructure, once the paperwork is done

heading_path: Stock clichés we do not use
results.content:
## Stock clichés we do not use

These are banned in every Wickhold image, photographs above all:

- Hooded hackers, or any faceless figure at a keyboard in the dark
- Padlocks, physical or floating over a circuit board
- Glowing shields
- Matrix code, or any green-on-black rain of characters
- Blue server-room haze: aisles of racks lit cold blue, usually with fog or lens flare

The reason sits close to the voice. All five say "be afraid" or "we are a generic security vendor", and the brand exists to say neither. An engineer who sees a hooded figure on a Wickhold page will assume the rest of the page is equally lazy.

Close relatives count as the same failure: binary digits projected on a face, a globe wrapped in network lines, a hand reaching toward a holographic lock, a person in a suit pointing at a transparent screen.

## Judging library photos by eye

The library's metadata does not catch everything. Some old or off-brand photos are sitting in the library with an empty `restrictions` field, because nobody ever marked them. Some of them have sensible titles and tags. A clean record tells you nobody objected. You still have to look at the picture.

Open it at full size and ask:

1. **What color are the shadows?** Ours fall warm, toward brown or neutral. If the shadows go blue, it belongs to the 2024 era or to a stock site. The look of that era was bright, cold and very blue, and it clashes hard with Ember on the same page.
2. **Is the light real?** Even, shadowless light across a whole room means a set or a heavy edit.
3. **Is anybody posing?** Direct eye contact with the lens, crossed arms, a group laughing at a laptop: reject.
4. **Could this photo appear on any company's site?** If yes, reject it. We want to see a detail that belongs to this work.

If a photo fails one of these and has no restriction on it, do not use it, and tell Brand so the record can be updated. That second part helps the next person.

Examples from recent draft reviews:

| Draft used | Verdict | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Rack aisle, cold blue light, faint haze, no people | Rejected | Clean metadata, wrong look |
| Woman with headset smiling at the camera in a bright open office | Rejected | Posed and generic |
| Engineer's hands, laptop glow, dim closet behind | Approved | Warm, specific, one focal point |
| Three people at a whiteboard, one mid-gesture, late sun on the wall | Approved | Available light, real moment |

## Photos by setting

**Team and office.** Real desks, real clutter. Aim for moments between people, with one person clearly the focus of the frame. Conference-room shots work when something is happening on the table. The office kitchen works better than the boardroom.

**Infrastructure.** Shoot close. A patch panel with handwritten labels says more than a long aisle. Cables, breakers, fans, a rack door left open. Whatever the room's own lighting does, keep it warm in the edit, and if the room is lit cold and cannot be corrected, get closer to a warm lamp or drop the shot.

**Customer scenes.** The grocery distribution office, the credit union's back room, a store's network closet. These are the most valuable photos we have, since they show Kubernetes and its operators somewhere other than a startup. They also have the most paperwork behind them. A customer scene looks ordinary and that is the point: no hero angles.

**Remote on-call.** Kitchen tables and spare rooms, a laptop at dusk, a phone face-up beside it. On-call happens at home and most stock libraries do not show it. Keep faces turned away unless the person is a signed volunteer.

## Choosing for the audience

The same library serves different readers, so pick with them in mind.

- For platform engineers, prefer detail. A readable (and real) cable label will win more trust than any wide shot. Faces matter less.
- For CISOs, prefer a calm room and a person thinking. The frame should feel like a decision is being made. Skip anything that looks like a crisis in progress, including people crowding a screen.
- For a general or press audience, prefer one clear person doing one clear thing.

heading_path: Comments you will get in review
results.content:
## Comments you will get in review

"Too clean." The room looks unused. Find a frame with evidence of work.

"Whose laptop is that?" A third-party logo or a sticker with a company name is visible. Remove it or pick another frame.

"What's on the whiteboard?" Someone has to read it. Customer names and incident details are the usual finds.

"Cold." The white balance is off. If warming it makes skin go orange, the original light was wrong, so reshoot.

heading_path: What the metadata means for photos
results.content:
## What the metadata means for photos

All photographs carry `background: scene`. A photograph keeps its environment: we do not cut people or objects out of their rooms, and we do not swap the sky through an office window. If you need a subject on a plain ground, you need an illustration.

Most photos are 1536x1024 landscape, with a few 1024x1536 portrait. Check `width` and `height` before you plan a layout around one. Upscaling a photo by more than about 20% shows.

`safe_on` is mostly `any` for photos, since a scene brings its own ground. A photo edge can still fight the layout. A dark, underexposed photo set straight on Soot loses its edges entirely, so give it margin or move it to a Tallow section.

`source` will read `internal-production` for in-house work, and `attribution` is often empty. We do not run photographer credits.

## Cropping

Crops are allowed and usually needed, because different placements want different shapes. Keep the focal point inside the middle two-thirds of the frame, so a further crop by a platform does not cut it off. Do not crop a person at the neck or the wrist. Rotation is limited to straightening a horizon by a degree or two.

## Light editing only

Allowed: exposure, white balance toward warm, gentle contrast, removing a stray sticky note with a password on it, removing a third-party logo from a laptop lid.

Not allowed: adding screens, adding people, removing people from a group shot to work around a restriction, adding atmosphere (smoke, glow, flares), or replacing what is on a monitor with invented UI. If a monitor needs to show the product, use a real capture composited at the correct perspective, reviewed by Brand. We tried fake monitor content in a March shoot and engineers spotted the impossible kubectl output within a day.

Keep the original. Save an edit as a new library record with `variant_of` set to the original, so the restrictions on the source can be traced.

## Shooting new photos

If you are booking a shoot, the brief should cover:

- Named location and who there has agreed to it
- A shot list of six to ten moments, written as things happening rather than as poses
- A warning to everyone to clear whiteboards, sticky notes and screens of customer names, credentials and anything from an active incident
- Who will enter the metadata. Files without a record do not enter the library

Shoot in the afternoon if you have a choice. Morning light in the Denver office is cold, and it takes more work to bring back to our look than it is worth.

Phone photos are welcome if they meet the look. Some of our best library images came from an engineer's phone in a colocation facility. Send the original file, not a screenshot of a chat.

## Things we tried and dropped

**Black-and-white.** Trialed for the founder story in spring. It looked serious and lost the warmth that sets us apart from the rest of the category.

**Ember color wash over photos.** Looked like a concert poster, and it tinted skin badly.

**Close-ups of fire.** One literal candle shot made the rebrand launch. After that the joke was used up, and flames in photographs began to read as disaster. A flame belongs in illustration, where it stays small.

**Drone shots of data centers.** Anonymous, and they could belong to anyone. They also raised a question about which site it was, which we could not answer.

# Product UI screenshots

Product marketing, with design review from Brand. Current as of the September release.

Screenshots are the one kind of image a platform engineer will inspect closely. They will read the pod names and check whether the timestamps make sense. Treat every screenshot as a claim about the product, because that is how it gets read.

## Where screenshots come from

Screens are captured from the product running in the demo environment, or rendered from the demo environment's HTML with Playwright at 1600x1000. Library dashboards are that size and opaque.

Never capture from:

- A customer tenant, even with their permission and even if you blur things
- Our own production tenant, which contains real incidents and real people's names
- A design file. Mockups of features that do not exist are not screenshots. If we need to show something unreleased, it must be labeled as a concept and approved by product marketing and Legal
- A model. Interface images are never generated

Do not paint over or blur a screenshot to hide data. Blurred regions imply the original had something worth hiding. Fix the demo data and take it again.

## Demo data

The demo environment is seeded with fictional clusters, namespaces and workloads. Keep it believable:

- Cluster and namespace names that look like real engineers wrote them: `payments-prod`, `batch-eu`, `ingest`. No `foo`, no `test123`, and nothing funny at a customer's expense
- Container images under `registry.wickhold.example`, so no real image names or registries appear
- People's names, where the screen shows an assignee, from the fictional demo roster. Do not use real staff, because staff leave. No names of customers, approved or otherwise
- Timestamps that agree with each other. An alert cannot be contained before it fired
- CVE IDs only when they are real, public and old. Do not imply a live incident

**Numbers on screen are claims.** A tile that shows a time to contain, a CPU figure or a count of findings fixed will be read as a result. Demo values must not look like a customer result or undercut an approved figure. If a tile reads like a brag, change the seed data, or crop it out. If you want to make a performance point, use an approved claim in the copy and keep it out of the picture.

Pricing and contract screens are never captured. Discount fields, billing pages and node counts tied to a plan stay out of marketing images.

## What to show

Each screenshot shows one action or one finding. That's the focal point, and the crop should make it obvious. Good subjects:

**Quenchline**
- One containment action in progress: isolating a pod's network, freezing a process, or draining a node
- The default containment policy view, with one rule highlighted
- Contain mode and observe mode side by side only if the page is explaining the difference. Otherwise pick one

**Evenburn**
- One piece of drift, showing expected and actual values
- An exposure path from a public entry point to a workload, short enough to read
- A fix order list, top three items

**Leashgate**
- One tool-call policy and the call it blocked or allowed
- An agent identity record
- The early access pill in the product header stays in frame. Do not crop it off

Avoid the whole-dashboard overview shot unless the point is the overview. A full 1600x1000 frame, shrunk to fit a column, is a gray rectangle full of illegible numbers.

## Cropping and framing

- Crop to the region that carries the point. Keep enough surrounding UI so that a reader knows where they are, usually the page title and one neighboring panel
- If UI text is too small to read at the published size, crop tighter or use a different screen
- No fake browser chrome and no device mockups. A floating laptop with a screenshot on it adds a second object and looks like a template
- No perspective tilts or 3D rotation
- Square corners, unless the layout's image style rounds everything equally
- A 1px Whetstone border is allowed when a screen with a light UI sits on Tallow and the edge gets lost

The interface has its own colors and they stay as they are. Do not recolor UI to suit a layout. Do not swap state colors to make something look calmer than it is.

## Annotations

Annotations are added in the design tool, on a separate layer, after the capture. One callout is usually enough, three at the most.

- Callouts use IBM Plex Sans in sentence case
- One Ember ring or arrow marks the focal area. No red boxes, no hand-drawn circles, no numbered badges over the UI
- Describe what happened. "Network isolated in this step" is good. "Instant protection!" is bad
- Commands and flags in callouts use IBM Plex Mono and must be real. Run them first

Example callouts:

| Good | Bad |
|---|---|
| Contain mode freezes the process and keeps its evidence | Stops every attack automatically |
| Drift found on 3 nodes, first in fix order | Full visibility across everything |
| Tool call denied by policy | AI threats eliminated |

## Terminals and CLI output

Engineers often trust a terminal capture over a dashboard. Use a plain terminal at a normal size with IBM Plex Mono, on a Soot background, with the prompt trimmed to `$`. The command has to be real and its output has to be pasted from a real run in the demo environment. Do not edit output to shorten it. Use `...` on its own line if you must cut something, and do so only where the cut changes nothing. Remove usernames, internal hostnames and tokens by fixing the environment and running it again.

## One screen, worked through

The request: show that Quenchline can freeze a process during an incident.

First attempt: the whole incident page at 1600x1000, with the timeline, three tiles, a side panel of pod details and a chat widget from the demo tenant. As a column image it was unreadable, and the one thing that mattered was a small status chip.

Second attempt: a crop to the timeline row showing the containment action and the status chip, with the page title kept above it. One Ember ring on the chip. One callout: "Process frozen, evidence kept". It reads at column width and it says one thing. That is the standard to aim for.

## Keeping screenshots current

Screens age quickly, and old ones do damage in specific ways:

- **Before March 2026, Evenburn screens carry the product's previous name** in the navigation and page titles. Check `added_date` and look at the header. A screen with the old name is unusable, even when the part you want is elsewhere in the frame. Crop-around is not a fix, since the layout and colors are dated too.
- **Before the February 2026 rebrand, the product UI used the old blue theme and the old logo** in the corner. Same answer.
- **Removed features.** Product marketing reviews the library's screenshots against the release notes at each major release, and adds a `restrictions` note to anything that no longer matches.

If a screenshot's record is clean and the picture still looks out of date against the live product, trust your eyes and take a fresh one. The demo environment is reset each Monday, so captures are straightforward. Anything that shows a feature's name, a label or a flow that has changed needs replacing before the next use.

## Metadata for new captures

Every new capture gets a record with `background` set, `source: internal-production`, the product name in `tags`, the release in `description`, and any limits in `restrictions`. If a capture shows a beta feature, say so in `restrictions`, with the date it should be reviewed.

## Video and GIF

Short looping captures follow all of the rules above. Each should show one action from start to finish in under ten seconds. Motion rules sit with the accessibility notes.

## Who signs off

Product marketing checks accuracy. Brand checks the crop and annotations. If a screenshot shows a feature that engineering has not shipped to all customers, the product manager for that area also signs off. Allow two working days.

# Social graphics

For anything designed for a feed: stat cards, quote cards, announcement cards, event cards. A plain photo or a plain chart uploaded to a post is covered by its own category. This page is about designed layouts.

Last touched by the social lead, May 2026. Kofi's team added the engineering post notes.

## Templates first

The library holds a small set of social templates, built in HTML and rendered with Playwright so the type is live and the layout stays exact. Start from one. Copy it, change the content, render it. A file marked as a template is a master and should not be posted unfilled.

Do not rebuild a template in a slide app. That is where off-size margins and the wrong weight of Bricolage Grotesque come from.

If you need a layout the templates do not cover, ask a designer. Do not stretch the stat card to hold a quote.

## Card types

**Stat card.** One number, a short line that says what it measures, and a source. Number in Bricolage Grotesque, very large. Use approved figures only, and keep the wording of an approved stat intact when you shorten it for a card. "7.4 hours" with "median time to contain a runtime incident" beneath it is fine. "Teams are failing at containment" is not what the number says.

**Quote card.** Customer quotes come from approved customers only. Use the quote as approved, without trimming it to sound stronger. Add the name, title and company as they were approved. Portraits are optional, and a portrait has its own consent requirements, separate from approval of the words. Founder quotes follow the same layout.

**Announcement card.** A short headline in sentence case on Tallow or Soot, plus the logo. For a release, name the capability and skip the excitement. "Wickhold Evenburn now shows exposure paths across clusters" is a good model. "Big news coming your way!" is the opposite.

**Event card.** Name, date, city. Slow Burn Summit and Field Day have a shared treatment, set with the events team each year.

## Layout

Each card has one Ember element, and on a card that element is usually a short rule beside the headline or the wick dot. The layout's text is never in Ember. Keep a clear margin all around, because platforms crop and round corners differently.

Logo placement is bottom right on Tallow and Soot cards.

Grounds: Tallow or Soot. Photos may be used in the right-hand half of the split layout, and text never overlaps a busy image. An abstract background from the library is allowed behind type, and it counts as the ground.

Keep the type large. Assume the card is viewed on a phone, in a feed, by someone with a thumb already moving. If you have reduced the font to fit the words, cut words.

## Copy on cards

Cards follow the voice rules with no special allowance for being short. Good:

- Small fires stay small.
- 11 minutes to contain, down from 4 hours.
- Contain mode, explained.

Bad:

- Hackers never sleep. Neither do we.
- The future of cloud security is HERE!
- Is your cluster on fire right now?

The 11-minute line needs Lowmoor named in the post or on the card, so that the number has a source.

A card should not repeat the post word for word. Use the post to expand on the card.

## Engineering posts

For posts aimed at platform engineers, a clean terminal or YAML snippet is often better than a designed card. Set it in IBM Plex Mono on a Soot ground, in a real, tested snippet of no more than twelve lines. Dry humor in a code comment is acceptable. Check the audience first.

```yaml
# drains the node. does not drain your weekend.
spec:
  action: drain-node
  mode: contain
```

Code cards still get checked by someone who can run them. This is a sample of the style, and its field names are not a reference.

## Common rejections

| What came in | What we said |
|---|---|
| Stat with no source anywhere | Add the source in the post or the card, or drop it |
| Ember headline on Tallow | Fails contrast. Use Soot, and keep Ember for the rule |
| Three stats on one card | Pick one. Post the others another day |
| Portrait, quote, logo and a screenshot together | Four focal points. Keep the quote |
| Card reused from before the rebrand | Rebuild it from the current template |
| Customer logo added to a stat card | Needs Legal first. Usually the answer is to name them in the post |

## Timing and thumbnails

Check every card at thumbnail size before you schedule it, and on a dark-theme feed as well as a light one. A Tallow card is a bright rectangle in a dark feed and that works in our favor. A Soot card can melt into the page, so keep its margin clean and its type large. Do not add a border to compensate.

## Series and carousels

We tried multi-slide carousels through Q1 and got poor completion on anything past the third slide, and each one ate a designer's afternoon. They are no longer part of the plan unless the social lead asks for one. Numbered series ("3 of 5") read as content for its own sake, so run a single good post instead.

## Sensitive moments

Check the news before a scheduled card goes out. A cheerful release card next to a public incident in our field looks careless. Hold it and ask. Illustrated flames and fire language are the first things to pull.

## Staff reshares

Staff may reshare cards as they are. Please ask them not to crop the logo or add filters. Sales teams sometimes make their own versions, and we would rather they ask. If you see a home-made card with an old logo or old colors, send it to Brand and leave the person alone. Usually they found an old file in a shared folder.

## Filing

Published cards are saved back to the library with a record. Set `restrictions` if a card carries a dated event or a time-limited statistic, so that nobody reuses it next year.

# Wickhold voice and tone

Noor Eskelund, Head of Brand. Written for the February 2026 rebrand, rewritten in April after the Containment Report went out, last edited in June. Comments go to #brand-review in Slack.

## Start at 3am

Anyone who writes for Wickhold should read an incident channel before writing a line of copy. Kofi Anselm's team keeps a few scrubbed transcripts for new hires. Skip the panic at the top of the thread and find the messages from whoever is running the incident. They tend to look like this:

> 03:14 UTC. A pod in `checkout` started a shell it has no reason to start.
> 03:14 UTC. Wickhold Quenchline froze the process and isolated the pod's network.
> 03:22 UTC. Rest of the namespace is quiet. Still unknown how the shell got there.
> Reading the image history now. Next update 03:45.

That is the voice. It says what happened, what is contained and what is next, in that order, and it stops. It has timestamps where other writers have adjectives. It admits the thing it does not know in the same flat tone as the thing it does. The person writing it is tired and is not going to make their tiredness your problem. Forty people are reading, half of them frightened, and the frightened ones calm down because of how the message is written.

Maren Tolliver and Dov Achterberg were on-call infrastructure leads before they founded this company in Denver in 2019. The voice is theirs by inheritance. The 2026 brand made it official: a wick is the one place a fire is allowed to exist. Production will catch fire in small ways, on ordinary nights, for dull reasons. The mission is to keep small failures from becoming big ones, and the copy should sound like it was written by people who consider that a normal day's work.

## The character

Wickhold is someone who has been paged more often than you have and is not going to bring it up.

**Unhurried.** Nothing in our copy is urgent. A page that hurries the reader is using the same trick as the alert fatigue they came to us to get away from.

**Exact.** "Isolated the pod's network" beats "took action". "220 nodes" beats "at scale". If two engineers would argue over what a sentence means, it isn't finished.

**Unimpressed by itself.** The product is useful. Copy that gasps at it reads as though the writer has not seen it fail. We have seen it fail, and the release notes say so.

**On your side of the pager.** The reader is a peer on the same rota, and we write to them as someone who could take the next shift. No lecturing, no "did you know", no explaining Kubernetes to people who run it.

When the character slips, it usually slips into one of four people:

- **The hero.** Rushes in, saves the day, gets the credit. Early rebrand drafts leaned on firefighters and helmets until Maren pointed out that a firefighter arriving means it already went badly. The customer's on-call team is the competent party in every story we tell.
- **The prophet.** Sees doom everywhere and sells shelter from it. The whole security industry's default register, which makes it invisible to the people we want to reach.
- **The buddy.** "Hey there, Kubernetes friends." Nobody paged at 3am wants a pal.
- **The analyst.** "In today's rapidly evolving threat landscape." Sentences with no one in them. If nothing would change when the paragraph is deleted, delete it.

## What Wickhold believes

These are opinions and we expect some readers to disagree with them. Copy that could have come from any vendor in the category has failed, even if it breaks no rule.

heading_path: Fear is not a sales tool
results.content:
### Fear is not a sales tool

No threat-actor drama. No ticking clocks.

The rule is simple to state and gets broken constantly, because fear copy is the easiest copy in security to write. It covers attackers portrayed as characters with motives and nicknames, anything of the "while you read this" kind, countdowns, "it's only a matter of time", "every second counts", and any sentence that asks the reader to imagine the phone call to the board. Our readers carry a pager. They do not need help imagining it.

Give the same fact without the dread.

Bad: "Attackers are already inside your cluster, and the clock is ticking."

Good: "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]."

The second sentence is more uncomfortable than the first, and it did not raise its voice. Trust the number to do that work.

Breach references have their own rules in the claims document. Read them before you mention one.

### Containment is the whole argument

Something will get through. Every serious engineer already knows this, and the companies who claim otherwise are talking to someone else. Wickhold's position is that the useful question is how far a failure gets and how fast it stops spreading. The whole product line follows from that, and so does most of our vocabulary. If a draft reads as though nothing bad will ever happen to the customer, it's arguing for a different company.

### Say the number, then stop

Claims carry a figure and a source. No adjective stacks.

"Fast" is not a claim. "A fast, powerful, highly scalable runtime platform" is three non-claims in a row. Write the number, say where it came from, and end the sentence. The urge to add a second sentence explaining why the number is impressive is the urge to resist. A reader who needs that sentence is the wrong reader; a reader who doesn't will think less of us for it.

Bad: "Lowmoor Credit Union saw an incredible, game-changing reduction in response times."

Good: "Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes across 220 nodes."

Bad: "Quenchline is extremely lightweight and blazingly quick."

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026."

If there is no figure, there is usually no claim, and the honest move is to describe what the product does in plain mechanical terms. "Isolates a pod's network" needs no number and no source. It's a description. "Industry-leading isolation" needs both and has neither.

### Admit limits

One of the company values, and the one marketing finds hardest. Every product we sell has an edge. Wickhold Evenburn finds drift and exposure paths; it does not contain anything. Quenchline contains what is running; it does not patch the image it came from. Saying so costs a little in the moment and buys a lot of belief for the next claim on the page. Engineers look for the catch. When they find we already named it, they keep reading.

### Specifics outrank concepts

Nobody's bad night was ever improved by a concept. Where a sentence can hold a pod, a node, a policy or a flag, put one in. "Runtime visibility" is a concept. "Which process opened that socket, and when" is something a person wants to know.

## Founder voice and brand voice

There are two voices at Wickhold, and they have one hard line between them.
